title: 13  Interval
section: 13.2 The middle half of each group
text:
13.2 The middle half of each group
A minimum and a maximum each come from a single row, so one unusual flower can set the whole whisker. To show the middle of a group instead of its extremes, give range two quantiles:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(iris_flowers) + interval * range(0.25, 0.75) + x(species) + y(petal_length) +
  x_label("Species") + y_label("Petal length (cm)") +
  title("Middle half of petal length per species")


(data(iris_flowers) + interval * range(0.25, 0.75) + x(col.species) + y(col.petal_length) +
  x_label("Species") + y_label("Petal length (cm)") +
  title("Middle half of petal length per species"))


data(iris_flowers) + interval * range(0.25, 0.75) + x(:species) +
  y(:petal_length) + x_label("Species") + y_label("Petal length (cm)") +
  title("Middle half of petal length per species")


plot(data(iris_flowers), layer(interval, range(0.25, 0.75)),
  x(col.species), y(col.petal_length), x_label("Species"),
  y_label("Petal length (cm)"),
  title("Middle half of petal length per species"))






                                       setosa versicolor virginica   2 3 4 5 6  Middle half of petal length per species Petal length (cm) Species





“Given the iris flowers: intervals derived by range from 0.25 to 0.75, x is species, y is petal length.”
This spans the first quartile to the third, which is the interquartile range. range(0.1, 0.9) keeps the middle 80%, and any other pair works the same way. range written with no arguments means range(0, 1), so it still spans from the minimum to the maximum. Transforms gives the full account of the two arguments.

title: 13  Interval
section: 13.3 Three layers instead of one mark
text:
13.3 Three layers instead of one mark
A box draws five numbers in one mark, and you take all five or none. Draw the band and the full range as two layers, and the median as a third. You can give any of the three layers its own style, drop one, or replace one:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(iris_flowers) +
  interval * range + style(color = "darkgray") +
  interval * range(0.25, 0.75) + style(color = "steelblue", size = 8) +
  point * median + style(color = "gold", size = 5, opacity = 1) +
  x(species) + y(petal_length) +
  x_label("Species") + y_label("Petal length (cm)") +
  title("Petal length per species, drawn in three layers")


(data(iris_flowers) +
  interval * range + style(color = "darkgray") +
  interval * range(0.25, 0.75) + style(color = "steelblue", size = 8) +
  point * median + style(color = "gold", size = 5, opacity = 1) +
  x(col.species) + y(col.petal_length) +
  x_label("Species") + y_label("Petal length (cm)") +
  title("Petal length per species, drawn in three layers"))


data(iris_flowers) + interval * range + style(color = "darkgray") +
  interval * range(0.25, 0.75) + style(color = "steelblue", size = 8) +
  point * median + style(color = "gold", size = 5, opacity = 1) +
  x(:species) + y(:petal_length) + x_label("Species") +
  y_label("Petal length (cm)") +
  title("Petal length per species, drawn in three layers")


plot(data(iris_flowers), layer(interval, range),
  style({ color: "darkgray" }), layer(interval, range(0.25, 0.75)),
  style({ color: "steelblue", size: 8 }), layer(point, median),
  style({ color: "gold", size: 5, opacity: 1 }), x(col.species),
  y(col.petal_length), x_label("Species"), y_label("Petal length (cm)"),
  title("Petal length per species, drawn in three layers"))






                                                   setosa versicolor virginica   2 4 6  Petal length per species, drawn in three layers Petal length (cm) Species





“Given the iris flowers: intervals derived by range, and also intervals derived by range from 0.25 to 0.75, and also points derived by median, x is species, y is petal length.”
The gray whisker is the full range, the thick blue band is the middle half, and the gold dot is the median. Order decides what you can see. A later layer is painted over an earlier one, so the median is written last. Move it to the front of the sentence and the band draws over it, leaving almost nothing to see. If you have used ggplot2, this is the rule you already know: a geom_ added later draws on top. The dot is set opaque as well, since every mark is slightly translucent by default.
The three layers name the three statistics, and a box plot draws the same three and names none of them. This is not a box redrawn, though, and the difference is at the ends. A box stops its whiskers at a cutoff computed from the quartiles, and draws every point beyond that cutoff as an outlier. A box on this same data draws outlier dots for setosa and versicolor. They are absent here, because these whiskers run to the true minimum and maximum.
Because each statistic is its own layer, you can change one without touching the others. Widen the band to range(0.1, 0.9) and the plot reports a different statistic, with the same marks. Drop the gray layer and the y axis is scaled to the band rather than to the extremes. Add a third layer with another pair of quantiles, and you have the fan chart drawn over categories instead of along a line. A box is still the shorter sentence when you want the five numbers and the outlier rule together.

title: 13  Interval
section: 13.4 A confidence interval, with a center
text:
13.4 A confidence interval, with a center
How well is the average petal length of each species known? That is a different question from how far the flowers spread, and it needs a different statistic. range shows the full spread. For the uncertainty of the mean, use confidence. It computes a t-interval for each group’s mean, which is the confidence interval the opening named, and that interval widens when the group is small. It keeps the mean as the center of the span, and the mark draws a dot there. A whisker with a dot at its center is a pointrange.


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(iris_flowers) + interval * confidence(0.95) + x(species) + y(petal_length) +
  x_label("Species") + y_label("Petal length (cm)") +
  title("95% CI of mean petal length")


(data(iris_flowers) + interval * confidence(0.95) + x(col.species) + y(col.petal_length) +
  x_label("Species") + y_label("Petal length (cm)") +
  title("95% CI of mean petal length"))


data(iris_flowers) + interval * confidence(0.95) + x(:species) +
  y(:petal_length) + x_label("Species") + y_label("Petal length (cm)") +
  title("95% CI of mean petal length")


plot(data(iris_flowers), layer(interval, confidence(0.95)),
  x(col.species), y(col.petal_length), x_label("Species"),
  y_label("Petal length (cm)"), title("95% CI of mean petal length"))






                                        setosa versicolor virginica   2 3 4 5  95% CI of mean petal length Petal length (cm) Species





“Given the iris flowers: intervals derived by confidence at 95%, x is species, y is petal length.”
The level is the only parameter, so confidence(0.99) draws wider than confidence(0.95). confidence computes a t-interval and takes no other. For a z-interval, a bootstrap, or the standard errors a model already gave you, compute the two numbers yourself and pass them to bounds.

title: 13  Interval
text:
13.5 The spread of the data
How far is a typical flower from the average of its species? That is a question about the spread of the data, not about how well the average is known. The opening of this chapter named three quantities: a standard deviation, a standard error and a confidence interval. confidence draws the confidence interval. The standard deviation has a transform of its own, deviation:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(iris_flowers) + interval * deviation + x(species) + y(petal_length) +
  x_label("Species") + y_label("Petal length (cm)") +
  title("Mean petal length, with one standard deviation")


(data(iris_flowers) + interval * deviation + x(col.species) + y(col.petal_length) +
  x_label("Species") + y_label("Petal length (cm)") +
  title("Mean petal length, with one standard deviation"))


data(iris_flowers) + interval * deviation + x(:species) +
  y(:petal_length) + x_label("Species") + y_label("Petal length (cm)") +
  title("Mean petal length, with one standard deviation")


plot(data(iris_flowers), layer(interval, deviation), x(col.species),
  y(col.petal_length), x_label("Species"), y_label("Petal length (cm)"),
  title("Mean petal length, with one standard deviation"))






                                          setosa versicolor virginica   2 3 4 5 6  Mean petal length, with one standard deviation Petal length (cm) Species





“Given the iris flowers: intervals derived by deviation, x is species, y is petal length.”
deviation alone reaches one standard deviation on each side of the mean. deviation(2) reaches two, so that band is four standard deviations wide. Like confidence it carries a center, so it draws a pointrange rather than a bare whisker.
The standard error has no transform of its own, and it does not need one. It is the standard deviation divided by the square root of the group size. confidence computes it internally and reports the interval built from it, which is what a reader of the plot needs.
deviation and confidence look alike and answer different questions. | puts two plots side by side on one page, and because both name petal_length on y they share that scale, drawn once down the left. The same operator splits one plot into panels when facet() is on its right instead, and Composition and Faceting have the rules for each. Here are the two statistics on the same fifty flowers per species:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


(data(iris_flowers) + interval * deviation + x(species) + y(petal_length) +
   y_label("Petal length (cm)") + title("Spread of the data")) |
  (data(iris_flowers) + interval * confidence + x(species) + y(petal_length) +
     y_label("") + title("Uncertainty of the mean"))


((data(iris_flowers) + interval * deviation + x(col.species) + y(col.petal_length) +
   y_label("Petal length (cm)") + title("Spread of the data")) |
  (data(iris_flowers) + interval * confidence + x(col.species) + y(col.petal_length) +
     y_label("") + title("Uncertainty of the mean")))


(data(iris_flowers) + interval * deviation + x(:species) +
  y(:petal_length) + y_label("Petal length (cm)") +
  title("Spread of the data")) |
  (data(iris_flowers) + interval * confidence + x(:species) +
  y(:petal_length) + y_label("") + title("Uncertainty of the mean"))


beside(plot(data(iris_flowers), layer(interval, deviation),
  x(col.species), y(col.petal_length), y_label("Petal length (cm)"),
  title("Spread of the data")),
  plot(data(iris_flowers), layer(interval, confidence), x(col.species),
  y(col.petal_length), y_label(""), title("Uncertainty of the mean")))






                                        setosa versicolor virginica   2 4 6  Spread of the data Petal length (cm) Species


                                   setosa versicolor virginica    Uncertainty of the mean Species






“Given the iris flowers: intervals derived by deviation, x is species, y is petal length, beside intervals derived by confidence, x is species, y is petal length.”
The bands on the right are less than a third as long, and the data is identical. The ratio is the same in all three species. The two statistics do not contradict each other. deviation describes how far the flowers are from their average, and measuring more of them does not make that band shorter. confidence describes how precisely the average itself is known. More flowers make it shorter: four times as many flowers make it half as long. That ratio comes from the group size, fifty flowers per species.
So choose by the caption you would write under the plot. “A versicolor petal is usually within half a centimeter of its species average” describes the left panel. “The average versicolor petal is 4.26 cm, and the interval reaches 0.13 cm on either side” describes the right one. Reporting one and meaning the other is the mistake the name error bar allows, and the reason gog asks you to name the statistic.
Which band is shorter also depends on the group size. With fifty flowers per species the confidence band is much shorter, as the plot shows. With only a few flowers per species it can be the longer one, because a t-interval widens when the group is small.
Whether a center exists is decided by the statistic, not by a setting. confidence and deviation compute a mean and range does not. So the shape follows from the statistic: a bare error bar for range, a pointrange for the other two. A setting can hide an existing center, as Hiding the center dot shows, but no setting adds one to range. A second layer does. point * mean over interval * range draws the same pointrange, as Three layers instead of one mark shows with the median. See Transforms for the whole range family.

title: 13  Interval
text:
13.6 Why interval needs a transform
Every plot so far has named a transform, and the rule behind that is worth stating on its own. A bar needs no transform, because the grammar already supplies its baseline: zero. bar + x + y draws. An interval has no such default. A low and a high are two numbers, and a plain y() supplies one. So the shortest interval that will draw is a mark, two positions, and a transform that produces a range. That is its minimum syllable. Ask for an interval without a transform and the engine refuses the sentence rather than drawing an empty panel. What it refuses shows that refusal.
This is the design choice that keeps the channel vocabulary small. The obvious alternative would add ymin and ymax as two more channels meaningful to a single mark, and a box plot would need five channels. Instead a transform invents the extents, exactly as bin invents a count, so the channel set never grows. box and ribbon read the same low and high values. The pair transform bounds(lower, upper) takes a low and a high you already have as two columns of the table, and Horizontal whiskers draws a coefficient plot with it.

title: 13  Interval
text:
13.7 Horizontal whiskers
Whiskers turn horizontal for the reasons bars do: the names are long, or there are many of them. A list of rows is then easier to scan than a row of columns. An interval takes its orientation from the bindings, the way a bar and a box do. Put the categories on y and the measured column on x:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(iris_flowers) + interval * confidence(0.95) + x(petal_length) + y(species) +
  x_label("Petal length (cm)") + y_label("Species") +
  title("The same 95% CI, horizontal")


(data(iris_flowers) + interval * confidence(0.95) + x(col.petal_length) + y(col.species) +
  x_label("Petal length (cm)") + y_label("Species") +
  title("The same 95% CI, horizontal"))


data(iris_flowers) + interval * confidence(0.95) + x(:petal_length) +
  y(:species) + x_label("Petal length (cm)") + y_label("Species") +
  title("The same 95% CI, horizontal")


plot(data(iris_flowers), layer(interval, confidence(0.95)),
  x(col.petal_length), y(col.species), x_label("Petal length (cm)"),
  y_label("Species"), title("The same 95% CI, horizontal"))






                                        2 3 4 5   virginica versicolor setosa  The same 95% CI, horizontal Species Petal length (cm)





The caps turn too, since a cap always crosses the span at its end. The center dot stays at the center. Everything else in this chapter is unchanged: pattern, color and dodge behave the same whichever axis carries the categories, and so do caps and center, the two settings that Caps, or a linerange and Hiding the center dot explain.
This is the usual shape for a coefficient plot, where each row is a named estimate and the reader reads down the list of intervals. Estimates like these normally arrive already computed, from a model rather than from raw observations. That is what bounds is for: it reads two columns you already have as the low and the high, and computes nothing. The terms go on y. bounds supplies the values for the other axis, so there is no x() to write:

An interval needs a number to span, so two categorical axes are refused, as they are on a bar and a box. What it refuses shows that refusal.

title: 13  Interval
text:
13.8 Splitting by color
A color says which whisker is which without reading the axis. The x axis already carries one category, so a channel is what separates a second one. color splits an interval into one whisker per group, the same categorical split line and bar make. The statistic is computed inside each group, so every group gets its own interval and its own hue. One legend names all of them:

13.9 Caps, or a linerange
The caps are the short lines across each end of a whisker. They are decoration rather than data, because they only emphasize where a whisker stops, and a crowded plot often reads more cleanly without them. So whether to draw them is a setting. style(caps = FALSE) drops them for a linerange, a whisker with no caps. caps = TRUE, the default, keeps the capped error bar. Each layer names its own statistic. bar * mean reduces each group to one number, and interval * confidence(0.95) computes the interval around that number. Both read the same column and report different things, and the sentence says which is which. The dot is turned off because the top of the bar already marks the mean, and the engine draws the two at exactly the same height.
A bar with an error bar is the figure where the three quantities from the opening are most often confused. The whisker looks the same whether it is a standard deviation, a standard error or a confidence interval. A caption has to say which one it is, because the drawing cannot. In gog the sentence has already said it. This one names confidence(0.95), and deviation in its place would give a different sentence and a much longer whisker.

Oceania has both the shortest whisker and the longest, from the same two countries. A confidence interval from two values is wide, because two values say little about the spread. title: 13  Interval
text:
13.15 In short
An interval is geometry and nothing else. The transform says which two numbers it spans, and whether there is a center to draw. Caps, the center dot and the dash are settings, so none of the three reads a column.

title: 13  Interval
text:
13.16 What comes next
Which two numbers an interval spans is the transform’s answer, never the mark’s. Box answers it inside the mark, with the five-number summary that gives the box plot its name.

title: 14  Box
text:
14.1 A summary per group
How is each group spread out? box draws the box-and-whisker of a distribution, one per group. In each category it summarizes the measured column. A box spans the lower quartile to the upper, with a line at the median. Whiskers reach to the most extreme values within 1.5 times the interquartile range (IQR) of the box. Any points beyond that are outliers, drawn individually as dots. bar * mean gives one number per group. box shows how the whole group is spread, and draws the few values far from the rest as separate dots. Boxes are vertical when the categories are on x and horizontal when they are on y; see Horizontal boxes.
The construction is John Tukey’s, from Exploratory Data Analysis (Tukey, 1977), where he called it a schematic plot. The name readers kept was his informal one, box-and-whisker, now usually shortened to box plot. Mary Eleanor Spear’s range bar of 1952 (Spear, 1952) had drawn the box and the extremes a quarter century earlier. The range bar had no rule for the fence, the cutoff that decides which values are outliers. That rule, 1.5 times the IQR, is Tukey’s, and so is the choice of where ordinary values stop and unusual ones begin.
There is one difference from his book. Tukey’s box spans hinges. Sort the values, cut the sorted list in half, and take the median of each half. gog spans the lower and upper quartiles instead, as most software does. The two agree when a group has an odd number of values and differ slightly when the number is even. A box drawn by gog is therefore not always the box Tukey’s own rule gives.
How do the three species differ in petal length, not only on average but in how widely each varies? Put the category that splits the data on x, and put the measured column on y. The mark computes the summary itself:

14.3 Horizontal boxes
When the category names are long, or there are many of them, the boxes should be horizontal. Swap the two positions, and the same sentence draws the same plot with the two axes exchanged. If you know ggplot2’s coord_flip(), there is no such word here, for the same reason bar has none. gog reads the two bindings and decides from them which axis carries the numbers. A second way to say one thing is a second thing to learn.

  x_label("Life expectancy (years)"), y_label("Continent"),
  title("The same five distributions, horizontal"))

title: 14  Box
text:
14.4 Whiskers to the extremes
Sometimes you do not want outliers drawn separately. You want the whiskers to run to the true minimum and maximum, the plain five-number summary. That is the one parameter the box mark carries, box(whiskers = "range"):


RPythonJuliaJavaScript

  title("The same, with whiskers to the full range")


(data(gapminder_2007) + box(whiskers = "range") + x(col.continent) + y(col.life) +
  x_label("Continent") + y_label("Life expectancy (years)") +
  title("The same, with whiskers to the full range"))


data(gapminder_2007) + box(whiskers = "range") + x(:continent) +
  y(:life) + x_label("Continent") + y_label("Life expectancy (years)") +
  title("The same, with whiskers to the full range")

  y(col.life), x_label("Continent"), y_label("Life expectancy (years)"),
  title("The same, with whiskers to the full range"))

“Given gapminder 2007: boxes with whiskers to the range, x is continent, y is life.”
Now Afghanistan and Haiti are the ends of their whiskers rather than dots. No point is called an outlier. The default is "tukey": fences and outliers, the standard box plot. "range" is the whole five-number summary, with no value drawn as an outlier. whiskers is the only choice a box offers.

title: 14  Box
text:
14.5 Why box needs no transform
An interval cannot draw without a transform to give it a low and a high. A box never needs one. An interval is only a shape, a span from a low value to a high one. Which low and high it spans is a real choice: a min–max range, a confidence interval, or a precomputed pair. A box is a named statistical glyph: the summary is what a box plot means. A statistic that draws as exactly one mark belongs to that mark, not beside it as a transform you compose. So the whole box is box + x + y, and adding a transform to it is refused with direction, as What it refuses shows.
This is the principle that keeps the channel vocabulary small, applied to a mark instead of a channel. Borrowing ymin/ymax/lower/middle/upper as channels would add five channels meaningful to a single mark. Instead the summary is invented inside the mark, and the channel set never grows.
The difference is one row in a table. Three marks read a low and a high value from a transform, and the fourth carries its own:



Mark
The spread it draws




interval * range
a whisker from the low value to the high


ribbon * range
the band between them, filled


line * range
the two values as two separate strokes


box
the five-number summary, with no transform to write

title: 14  Box

14.6 Coloring the boxes
Three boxes in one color look like one series. A color per species lets a reader match each box to the same species in another plot. A color is also how a second category, such as an era, shares each slot. color gives each box its own hue and a legend, the same categorical split bar and interval make. Here color is mapped to the same column as x, so it colors one box per group:

  color(:species) + x_label("Species") + y_label("Petal length (cm)") +
  title("The same distributions, colored by species")

box is one of the distribution marks, and each of them answers a different question. bar * bin draws one variable’s histogram, and interval draws a range or an error bar. box gives the summary per group. The violin (ribbon * density) draws the whole distribution that summary is computed from. See Transforms for dodge, and for how mean, median and range differ from the box’s own summary.

  style(pattern = "dashed")

  style({ pattern: "dashed" }))

A transform is the fourth. A box already summarizes each group into quartiles, a median and whiskers, so it takes none. Why box needs no transform gave the reason:

The message names the fix: drop the transform, and the box draws its own summary.

title: 14  Box
text:
14.9 In short
gog’s box spans the quartiles, and Tukey’s spans hinges, so on a group with an even number of values the two differ slightly. The summary is inside the mark: a box refuses every statistic, and takes only dodge, which moves boxes and computes nothing. whiskers is its one parameter. A box’s width is fixed by its slot, so no column can vary it.

title: 14  Box
text:
14.10 What comes next
A box occupies one position on its axis, and its width does not depend on the axis. Ribbon carries a spread along the whole axis, filling the band between a low boundary and a high one.




Spear, M. E. (1952). Charting statistics. McGraw-Hill.


Tukey, J. W. (1977). Exploratory data analysis. Addison-Wesley.

title: 15  Ribbon
text:
15.1 A band from a range
How wide is the band of values at each point along x? ribbon draws a filled band from a low boundary to a high one across x: a confidence band, a spread band, the shaded region around a trend. It fills one region, the way an area does. It reads a low value and a high value at each position, the way an interval does. An area fills from the data down to a baseline at zero. A ribbon has no baseline, and both of its edges are values the table supplies.
Did the five countries move closer together over the years, or further apart? The gap between the lowest and the highest in each year answers that. A band drawn between those two values shows every year at once, as one shape. The two boundaries come from a transform, exactly as an interval’s two extents do. range reduces y to its minimum and maximum within each x, and the ribbon fills between them. title: 15  Ribbon
text:
15.2 The mean and its band
On its own a band shows spread but not center. A band is usually drawn with a line through the middle. You compose the two by layering, not by adding an option to either mark. A ribbon * range for the spread, a line * mean for the trend, sharing one x and y:

  ribbon * range + style(color = "steelblue", opacity = 0.25) +

  y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("Mean life expectancy, with its min–max band")

  ribbon * range + style(color = "steelblue", opacity = 0.25) +
  line * mean + style(color = "steelblue", size = 2) +
  y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("Mean life expectancy, with its min–max band"))


data(gapminder_asia) + x(:year) + y(:life) + ribbon * range +
  style(color = "steelblue", opacity = 0.25) + line * mean +
  style(color = "steelblue", size = 2) + y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("Mean life expectancy, with its min–max band")


plot(data(gapminder_asia), x(col.year), y(col.life), layer(ribbon, range),
  style({ color: "steelblue", opacity: 0.25 }), layer(line, mean),
  style({ color: "steelblue", size: 2 }), y_label("Life expectancy"),
  title("Mean life expectancy, with its min–max band"))






                                  1960 1980 2000   40 50 60 70 80  Mean life expectancy, with its min–max band Life expectancy Year





“Given gapminder Asia: x is year, y is life, a ribbon derived by range and also a line derived by mean.”
Each layer runs its own transform on the same table. mean reduces each year to one point for the line, and range reduces the same year to a low and high pair for the band. This is the most common ribbon plot: a trend with its uncertainty or spread drawn around it. It is two marks the grammar already has, added with +.

The pale band contains the middle 80% of countries. The darker one contains the middle half, and the line is the median. The plot then says something the min–max version cannot. The median rose from 45 years to 72, and the 90th percentile from 67 to 80, so the distance between them fell from 22 years to 8.
The lower edges of the two bands do not rise steadily. Both lower edges, the 10th percentile and the 25th, decline between 1992 and 2002 while the median rises throughout. A min–max band cannot show this, because its lower edge is one country.
The same layering goes further. Each band is one more layer, so a third pair of quantiles adds a third band. Write the widest band first, because a later layer is painted over an earlier one.

title: 15  Ribbon
section: 15.4 Why a ribbon needs a transform
text:
15.4 Why a ribbon needs a transform
A low and a high are two numbers, and a plain y() supplies one. An area closes on zero, which the grammar supplies. A ribbon has no such second number, so like interval its minimum syllable includes a range-producing transform. Write a ribbon without such a transform and the engine refuses it, rather than drawing an empty panel. What it refuses shows the message.
This is the same design choice that keeps the channel vocabulary small. The alternative would add ymin and ymax as two more channels, and only one mark would ever use them. Instead the boundaries are invented by a transform, exactly as bin invents a count. The same low and high rows then serve the whisker, the box and the band. See Transforms for the range, confidence and deviation statistics.
Read the requirement as where do the two boundaries come from? rather than as a list of transforms. One answer is unlike the rest. density over a category gives a ribbon its boundaries by reflection, and that is the violin, at the end of this chapter.

title: 15  Ribbon
text:
15.5 A confidence band
How well is the mean life expectancy known in each year? That is a different question from how far the five countries spread. range shows the full spread. For the uncertainty of the mean, use confidence. It computes a t-interval for the mean at each x, and the ribbon fills between its two bounds. The interval widens when the group is small:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_asia) + ribbon * confidence(0.95) + x(year) + y(life) +
  y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("95% confidence band for mean life expectancy")


(data(gapminder_asia) + ribbon * confidence(0.95) + x(col.year) + y(col.life) +
  y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("95% confidence band for mean life expectancy"))


data(gapminder_asia) + ribbon * confidence(0.95) + x(:year) + y(:life) +
  y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("95% confidence band for mean life expectancy")


plot(data(gapminder_asia), layer(ribbon, confidence(0.95)), x(col.year),
  y(col.life), y_label("Life expectancy"),
  title("95% confidence band for mean life expectancy"))






                               1960 1980 2000   40 50 60 70 80  95% confidence band for mean life expectancy Life expectancy Year





“Given gapminder Asia: a ribbon derived by confidence at 95%, x is year, y is life.”
The band is wide because each mean comes from only five countries. Those five differ by more than fifteen years, so the interval around their mean is wide. A higher level draws a wider band still. What the band means is decided by the statistic you name: range draws the observed spread, and confidence draws the uncertainty of the mean. Neither one is a new mark to learn, which is the rule the interval family follows too.

title: 15  Ribbon
text:
15.6 A pre-computed band
range, confidence and deviation compute the band from raw values in the plot. Most confidence bands are not computed in the plot at all. A model’s standard error, a standard error of measurement, a bootstrap interval: each of these is computed before the plot. Its two bounds then become two columns in the table. gog draws what you computed, and it does not re-fit the model. The score_band table holds one row per raw test score. Each row also holds the score a model predicts for that raw score, and the two edges of the band around the prediction:

RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(score_band) + ribbon * bounds(lower, upper) + x(score) +
  y_label("Expected true score") + x_label("Raw score") +
  title("A pre-computed measurement band")


(data(score_band) + ribbon * bounds(col.lower, col.upper) + x(col.score) +
  y_label("Expected true score") + x_label("Raw score") +
  title("A pre-computed measurement band"))


data(score_band) + ribbon * bounds(:lower, :upper) + x(:score) +
  y_label("Expected true score") + x_label("Raw score") +
  title("A pre-computed measurement band")

  x(col.score), y_label("Expected true score"), x_label("Raw score"),
  title("A pre-computed measurement band"))

“Given the score band: a ribbon from lower to upper, x is score.”
bounds is range’s counterpart, and it computes nothing. It reshapes the two columns you give it into the same low and high pair range produces. The band needs no y(), because the two columns are the boundaries. This is the one case range, confidence and deviation cannot serve: a band that was computed outside the plot, before gog ever read the table.
A band like this is usually drawn together with the values it surrounds. Here those values are the expected true score, the score the model predicts for each raw score. A dashed line draws them, with a point at every raw score. The band, the line and the points are three layers composed with +:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(score_band) + x(score) + y(expected) +
  ribbon * bounds(lower, upper) + style(color = "steelblue", opacity = 0.18) +
  line + style(color = "steelblue", size = 1.4, pattern = "dashed") +
  point + style(color = "steelblue", size = 2.4) +
  y_label("Expected true score") + x_label("Raw score") +
  title("Expected score with its measurement error band")


(data(score_band) + x(col.score) + y(col.expected) +
  ribbon * bounds(col.lower, col.upper) + style(color = "steelblue", opacity = 0.18) +
  line + style(color = "steelblue", size = 1.4, pattern = "dashed") +
  point + style(color = "steelblue", size = 2.4) +
  y_label("Expected true score") + x_label("Raw score") +
  title("Expected score with its measurement error band"))


data(score_band) + x(:score) + y(:expected) +
  ribbon * bounds(:lower, :upper) +
  style(color = "steelblue", opacity = 0.18) + line +
  style(color = "steelblue", size = 1.4, pattern = "dashed") + point +
  style(color = "steelblue", size = 2.4) +
  y_label("Expected true score") + x_label("Raw score") +
  title("Expected score with its measurement error band")


plot(data(score_band), x(col.score), y(col.expected),
  layer(ribbon, bounds(col.lower, col.upper)),
  style({ color: "steelblue", opacity: 0.18 }), line,
  style({ color: "steelblue", size: 1.4, pattern: "dashed" }), point,
  style({ color: "steelblue", size: 2.4 }),
  y_label("Expected true score"), x_label("Raw score"),
  title("Expected score with its measurement error band"))






                                                         0 5 10 15 20   0 10 20  Expected score with its measurement error band Expected true score Raw score





“Given the score band: x is score, y is expected, a ribbon from lower to upper, and also a line and points.”
The dashed line is style(pattern = ). On a stroke the texture is a dash, so here it applies to the line and not to the band. The band takes the same setting, with different values. On a fill the texture is a hatch: "hatch", "crosshatch", "stripes", "grid" or "dots", never "dashed".

title: 15  Ribbon
text:
15.7 Filled, or two dashed edges
A band is a low/high pair, and the mark chooses how to draw it. This is the No Exceptions rule again: one bin draws as a bar chart, as a line and as a step histogram, and one pair draws in as many ways. ribbon fills the pair. A line traces its two boundaries instead, which is the unfilled band many journals prefer. With style(pattern = ) it becomes the dashed pair of curves those journals often print:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(score_band) + x(score) + y(expected) +
  line * bounds(lower, upper) + style(color = "gray", pattern = "dashed", size = 1.2) +
  line + style(color = "steelblue", size = 1.5) +
  point + style(color = "steelblue", size = 2.4) +
  y_label("Expected true score") + x_label("Raw score") +
  title("The same band, unfilled: two dashed edges")


(data(score_band) + x(col.score) + y(col.expected) +
  line * bounds(col.lower, col.upper) + style(color = "gray", pattern = "dashed", size = 1.2) +
  line + style(color = "steelblue", size = 1.5) +
  point + style(color = "steelblue", size = 2.4) +
  y_label("Expected true score") + x_label("Raw score") +
  title("The same band, unfilled: two dashed edges"))


data(score_band) + x(:score) + y(:expected) +
  line * bounds(:lower, :upper) +
  style(color = "gray", pattern = "dashed", size = 1.2) + line +
  style(color = "steelblue", size = 1.5) + point +
  style(color = "steelblue", size = 2.4) +
  y_label("Expected true score") + x_label("Raw score") +
  title("The same band, unfilled: two dashed edges")


plot(data(score_band), x(col.score), y(col.expected),
  layer(line, bounds(col.lower, col.upper)),
  style({ color: "gray", pattern: "dashed", size: 1.2 }), line,
  style({ color: "steelblue", size: 1.5 }), point,
  style({ color: "steelblue", size: 2.4 }),
  y_label("Expected true score"), x_label("Raw score"),
  title("The same band, unfilled: two dashed edges"))






                                                          0 5 10 15 20   0 10 20  The same band, unfilled: two dashed edges Expected true score Raw score





“Given the score band: x is score, y is expected, lines from lower to upper, and also a line and points.”
line * bounds is one layer that draws both edges, splitting the pair into a low curve and a high one. It therefore needs no second y. Two plain line layers can draw two columns you already have. They cannot split a pair that range computes, because that pair never becomes a column you can name. line * bounds reads any pair the same way. line * range traces a min–max envelope, and line * confidence traces the two edges of a confidence interval. step * bounds draws the same two edges as staircases. Filled or unfilled, solid or dashed, it is one pair and a choice of mark, never a new option added to the band.

How does the spread of one continent compare with another’s, year by year? One band per continent puts the three ranges in one panel. A categorical column splits a ribbon into one band per group. “Given the gapminder continents: ribbons derived by range, x is year, y is life, color by continent.”
The bands overlap where two continents cover the same range of life expectancy. A split area fills every region at the same opacity it uses for one, so only a little of the region behind shows through. The stack transform is an area’s answer to that: it starts each region at the top of the ones below, so no two regions overlap at all. A ribbon instead draws its split translucent by default, so a band behind another is still readable. The difference follows from what each mark measures. An area measures a height from the baseline, so its groups can be piled into a total. A ribbon already spans a low to a high and measures no such height, so there is nothing to stack. Overlapping bands are read through transparency and never stacked, which is why ribbon * stack is refused and the refusal names style(opacity = ).

title: 15  Ribbon
text:
15.9 One region, one fill
A ribbon is a single filled region, so opacity is a setting here, not a channel, exactly as on area. Each row of the table is one corner of a boundary, not a piece of the fill. No part of the band belongs to one row, so a column cannot make one row lighter or darker than another. What it refuses shows the refusal.
size cannot be set either. A band’s extent comes from its x and its two boundaries, so there is no width to choose. Its edge, if you want one, is a line layered along a boundary, never an outline option on the mark. That is the ribbon + line composition drawn in A pre-computed band.

text:

title: 15  Ribbon
section: 15.11 The violin: a distribution per category
text:
15.11 The violin: a distribution per category
A range on a category gives two numbers per group, the lowest and the highest. density gives a whole shape per group, and a ribbon has room for that shape. The estimate spreads along the measure. It is drawn across the category’s slot and mirrored, so the two halves are the same curve facing opposite ways. That is the violin plot (Hintze & Nelson, 1998), and it is this chapter’s sentence with one word changed:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + ribbon * density + x(continent) + y(life) +
  y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("ribbon * density: one distribution per continent")


(data(gapminder_2007) + ribbon * density + x(col.continent) + y(col.life) +
  y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("ribbon * density: one distribution per continent"))


data(gapminder_2007) + ribbon * density + x(:continent) + y(:life) +
  y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("ribbon * density: one distribution per continent")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(ribbon, density), x(col.continent),
  y(col.life), y_label("Life expectancy"),
  title("ribbon * density: one distribution per continent"))






                                   Asia Europe Africa Americas Oceania   40 60 80  ribbon * density: one distribution per continent Life expectancy Continent





“Given gapminder 2007: ribbons derived by density, x is continent, y is life.”
density is not the ribbon’s own transform. Five other marks estimate the same curve, and only the shape changes:



Mark derived by density
Shape




line * density
the curve as a stroke


step * density
the curve as a staircase


area * density
the curve filled to the baseline


point * density
one dot at each point the curve was estimated


bar * density
one thin bar at each of those points


ribbon * density
the curve mirrored, the violin above



line, step and area also read a category on one axis, exactly as the violin does. point and bar need a continuous axis instead: one dot or one thin bar per estimated point has no reading inside a category’s slot, so gog refuses both there.
Nothing new was added to the grammar to draw it. A ribbon closes on a second boundary the data supplies, and a violin closes on the mirror image of its own curve. density is the transform that estimates a distribution, and this plot is that estimate read per group. There is no violin word to learn. Such a word would have to say four things at once: the mark, the statistic, the mirror and the slot. Every one of those is already said by something you know.
Read it against the box of the same two columns. A box gives you five numbers you can name. The violin gives you the shape those five numbers summarize. Africa’s violin is widest near 52 years, and it has a second, smaller bulge near 73. Its median is 53, and a single number cannot report that second group at all.


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + box + x(continent) + y(life) +
  y_label("Life expectancy") + title("box + x + y: the same distributions, summarized")


(data(gapminder_2007) + box + x(col.continent) + y(col.life) +
  y_label("Life expectancy") + title("box + x + y: the same distributions, summarized"))


data(gapminder_2007) + box + x(:continent) + y(:life) +
  y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("box + x + y: the same distributions, summarized")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), box, x(col.continent), y(col.life),
  y_label("Life expectancy"),
  title("box + x + y: the same distributions, summarized"))






                                                                  Asia Europe Africa Americas Oceania   40 50 60 70 80  box + x + y: the same distributions, summarized Life expectancy Continent





“Given gapminder 2007: boxes, x is continent, y is life.”

15.11.1 What the width means
Every group’s density integrates to 1 on its own. If the estimate stopped there, the widths would say nothing about how many rows each group has. A continent of two countries would be drawn as wide as a continent of fifty-two. So by default the estimate is weighted by the group’s row count, and width means the same thing across the whole panel. Oceania holds two countries, so it is the narrowest violin in the plot above.
The weighting is on the shape’s area, not on its width, which is why Europe is drawn wider there than Africa. Europe’s thirty countries sit within ten years of each other, so Europe’s area is packed into a short stretch of the axis and the shape has to be wide. Africa’s fifty-two countries are spread over thirty-seven years, so a larger area is spread thin. What the width reports at any height is countries per year of life expectancy, and that reading is the same in every slot.
compare = "shape" removes that weighting and draws every violin to the same area. It is the right reading when the question is about the shapes alone. It is the wrong one when a group whose values are packed together takes the width away from every other violin:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + ribbon * density(compare = "shape") + x(continent) + y(life) +
  y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title('density(compare = "shape"): every violin the same area')


(data(gapminder_2007) + ribbon * density(compare = "shape") + x(col.continent) + y(col.life) +
  y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title('density(compare = "shape"): every violin the same area'))


data(gapminder_2007) + ribbon * density(compare = "shape") +
  x(:continent) + y(:life) + y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("density(compare = \"shape\"): every violin the same area")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(ribbon, density({ compare: "shape" })),
  x(col.continent), y(col.life), y_label("Life expectancy"),
  title("density(compare = \"shape\"): every violin the same area"))






                                   Asia Europe Africa Americas Oceania   40 60 80  density(compare = "shape"): every violin the same area Life expectancy Continent





“Given gapminder 2007: ribbons derived by density compared by shape, x is continent, y is life.”
Two countries now fill more space than fifty-two. Oceania’s two values are one year apart, so its equal share of area has to fit inside one year of the axis. The only way to fit that area there is to be very wide. The widest shape in a panel fixes the scale, so every other violin is drawn thinner against it. Each plot answers a different question, which is why the choice is a word you write rather than a default nobody stated.


15.11.2 Sideways, and halved
The category can go on either axis, and the violins turn to follow it. The orientation is read off the bindings, exactly as a bar’s or a box’s is. A category on y is the form with room for long category names:

  x_label("Life expectancy") + title("The same violins, turned sideways")

  x_label("Life expectancy") + title("The same violins, turned sideways"))

  x_label("Life expectancy") + title("The same violins, turned sideways")

  y(col.continent), x_label("Life expectancy"),
  title("The same violins, turned sideways"))

An area draws the same estimate closed on the slot’s center line instead of on its own reflection. So the area draws one side of the shape and the ribbon draws two, which is what separates these two marks everywhere else in the book:

  y_label("Life expectancy") + title("area * density: the half violin")

  y_label("Life expectancy") + title("area * density: the half violin"))

  y_label("Life expectancy") + title("area * density: the half violin")

  y(col.life), y_label("Life expectancy"),
  title("area * density: the half violin"))

“Given gapminder 2007: areas derived by density, x is continent, y is life.”
There are two choices here, and they are made independently: which mark closes the region, and which axis carries the category. That is four plots, and the fourth one has a name of its own. Halve the violin and turn it sideways. Each category then gets a filled curve on its own line above a shared measure axis, which is the ridgeline plot:

  x_label("Life expectancy") + title("area * density + x(life): the ridgeline")

  x_label("Life expectancy") + title("area * density + x(life): the ridgeline"))


data(gapminder_2007) + area * density + x(:life) + y(:continent) +
  x_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("area * density + x(life): the ridgeline")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(area, density), x(col.life),
  y(col.continent), x_label("Life expectancy"),
  title("area * density + x(life): the ridgeline"))






                                   40 60 80   Oceania Americas Africa Europe Asia  area * density + x(life): the ridgeline Continent Life expectancy





Nothing was added for it either. It is the half violin’s sentence with x and y exchanged. The plot exists because the two choices really are independent: nothing in the grammar ties where a region closes to which axis holds the category. All four combinations are sentences, and the named chart is simply one of them.
Read the four plots together and you can see what orthogonality gives you here. A word for the violin and a word for the ridgeline would be two names for one idea, and the other two combinations would have no word at all.


15.11.3 Letting the ridges overlap
The widest shape in a panel reaches four tenths of a slot by default, and every other shape is drawn to scale against it. Two of them in neighboring slots would reach four tenths each, filling four fifths of the space between their categories and leaving the last fifth empty. That is a bar’s rule, and for a bar’s reason: the gap is what marks the categories as separate rather than a divided continuum.
The ridgeline breaks that rule on purpose. As it is usually drawn (the form some call a joyplot) it does not stay inside its slot. Its ridges are tall enough to reach into the row above, and that overlap is part of the design. density(reach = ) says how far, in slots:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + area * density(reach = 2.5) + x(life) + y(continent) +
  x_label("Life expectancy") + title("reach = 2.5: each ridge two and a half slots tall")


(data(gapminder_2007) + area * density(reach = 2.5) + x(col.life) + y(col.continent) +
  x_label("Life expectancy") + title("reach = 2.5: each ridge two and a half slots tall"))


data(gapminder_2007) + area * density(reach = 2.5) + x(:life) +
  y(:continent) + x_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("reach = 2.5: each ridge two and a half slots tall")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(area, density({ reach: 2.5 })),
  x(col.life), y(col.continent), x_label("Life expectancy"),
  title("reach = 2.5: each ridge two and a half slots tall"))






                                   40 60 80   Oceania Americas Africa Europe Asia  reach = 2.5: each ridge two and a half slots tall Continent Life expectancy





“Given gapminder 2007: areas derived by density reaching 2.5 slots, x is life, y is continent.”
The number is measured from the line a category sits on to the shape’s furthest point. That is why the number means the same thing to both marks. A ribbon reaches that far on each side, an area on one side only. The half violin therefore stays exactly half of the violin, at any reach. Past 0.5 the shapes leave their own slots. The grammar does not guard against that. It is the plot being asked for, and the later category simply draws over the earlier one.
The category axis grows to hold the ridges. Half a slot of margin is right for a bar or a box, which stand in their slots. A ridge 2.5 slots tall does not stand in its slot, so the axis adds the room it needs. Without that room the panel edge would cut the top ridge off, and you would see the cut.
The edge is a layer here, as it is for every filled band in this chapter. A ribbon takes no border setting, and neither does the violin. A line given the same transform traces the outline of the fill. That is the Filled, or two dashed edges rule again, this time inside a category’s slot:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + x(life) + y(continent) +
  area * density(reach = 2.5) + style(color = "steelblue", opacity = 0.9) +
  line * density(reach = 2.5) + style(color = "black", size = 1) +
  x_label("Life expectancy") + title("The same ridges, with their edges drawn")


(data(gapminder_2007) + x(col.life) + y(col.continent) +
  area * density(reach = 2.5) + style(color = "steelblue", opacity = 0.9) +
  line * density(reach = 2.5) + style(color = "black", size = 1) +
  x_label("Life expectancy") + title("The same ridges, with their edges drawn"))


data(gapminder_2007) + x(:life) + y(:continent) +
  area * density(reach = 2.5) +
  style(color = "steelblue", opacity = 0.9) +
  line * density(reach = 2.5) + style(color = "black", size = 1) +
  x_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("The same ridges, with their edges drawn")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), x(col.life), y(col.continent),
  layer(area, density({ reach: 2.5 })),
  style({ color: "steelblue", opacity: 0.9 }),
  layer(line, density({ reach: 2.5 })),
  style({ color: "black", size: 1 }), x_label("Life expectancy"),
  title("The same ridges, with their edges drawn"))






                                          40 60 80   Oceania Americas Africa Europe Asia  The same ridges, with their edges drawn Continent Life expectancy





Both layers read the same density(reach = 2.5), so the stroke lands exactly on the edge of the fill it belongs to. That is the reason an edge is a layer rather than a setting. Color each ridge by its own category and the plot is complete:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + x(life) + y(continent) +
  area * density(reach = 2.2) + color(continent) +
  line * density(reach = 2.2) + style(color = "black", size = 0.9) +
  x_label("Life expectancy") + title("One hue per ridge")


(data(gapminder_2007) + x(col.life) + y(col.continent) +
  area * density(reach = 2.2) + color(col.continent) +
  line * density(reach = 2.2) + style(color = "black", size = 0.9) +
  x_label("Life expectancy") + title("One hue per ridge"))


data(gapminder_2007) + x(:life) + y(:continent) +
  area * density(reach = 2.2) + color(:continent) +
  line * density(reach = 2.2) + style(color = "black", size = 0.9) +
  x_label("Life expectancy") + title("One hue per ridge")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), x(col.life), y(col.continent),
  layer(area, density({ reach: 2.2 })), color(col.continent),
  layer(line, density({ reach: 2.2 })),
  style({ color: "black", size: 0.9 }), x_label("Life expectancy"),
  title("One hue per ridge"))






                                          40 60 80   Oceania Americas Africa Europe Asia  One hue per ridge Continent Life expectancy  Continent    Asia  Europe  Africa  Americas  Oceania 





The color(continent) is written after the area, so it belongs to that layer alone. Written before both marks it would color the line too, and a layer cannot both map color and set it. Where a channel sits in the sentence is what decides its scope, and Encoding scope explains that in full.
step * density traces the same estimate as a staircase, for the same reason step * bin is the outline histogram. No Exceptions means that a mark draws whatever rows a transform produces, in the mark’s own way.

title: 15  Ribbon
text:
15.12 What you can set
A setting changes how the band looks without reading a column, and each mark takes its own. These are a ribbon’s, with the values each accepts:







Setting
Value




style(color = )
any CSS color name or hex


style(opacity = )
0 to 1


style(pattern = )
solid, hatch, crosshatch, stripes, grid, dots



A ribbon takes area’s list, and for area’s reasons. There is no size, because the band’s extent comes from the two boundaries its transform supplies. There is no border, because the edge is a line traced along the same pair.
Here is the textured band with a line along both of its edges:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(score_band) + x(score) +
  ribbon * bounds(lower, upper) +
    style(color = "slateblue", pattern = "grid", opacity = 0.45) +
  line * bounds(lower, upper) + style(color = "slateblue", pattern = "dashed") +
  y_label("Expected true score") + title("A textured band, and its two edges")


(data(score_band) + x(col.score) +
  ribbon * bounds(col.lower, col.upper) +
    style(color = "slateblue", pattern = "grid", opacity = 0.45) +
  line * bounds(col.lower, col.upper) + style(color = "slateblue", pattern = "dashed") +
  y_label("Expected true score") + title("A textured band, and its two edges"))


data(score_band) + x(:score) + ribbon * bounds(:lower, :upper) +
  style(color = "slateblue", pattern = "grid", opacity = 0.45) +
  line * bounds(:lower, :upper) +
  style(color = "slateblue", pattern = "dashed") +
  y_label("Expected true score") +
  title("A textured band, and its two edges")


plot(data(score_band), x(col.score),
  layer(ribbon, bounds(col.lower, col.upper)),
  style({ color: "slateblue", pattern: "grid", opacity: 0.45 }),
  layer(line, bounds(col.lower, col.upper)),
  style({ color: "slateblue", pattern: "dashed" }),
  y_label("Expected true score"),
  title("A textured band, and its two edges"))






                                    0 5 10 15 20   0 10 20  A textured band, and its two edges Expected true score Score





“Given the score band: x is score, a ribbon from lower to upper, with pattern grid, and also lines from lower to upper, with pattern dashed.”
Both marks read the same bounds(lower, upper) there, exactly as the two ridge layers did, so the edges stay on the band. Note the two pattern values in one sentence. "grid" is a fill texture, and the ribbon is a fill. "dashed" is a stroke dash, and the line is a stroke. The setting has one name, and each geometry has its own set of values for it.
The grid of every mark and every setting shows which other marks share this list. What a mark maps rather than sets is its row on the companion grid.

title: 15  Ribbon
text:
15.13 What it refuses
The measure stays numeric. A band from range spans a low value to a high one, and both are quantities, so a category on y is refused. The violins above put a category on y, but there density makes it a slot rather than the measure:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + ribbon * range + x(life) + y(continent)


data(gapminder_2007) + ribbon * range + x(col.life) + y(col.continent)


data(gapminder_2007) + ribbon * range + x(:life) + y(:continent)


plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(ribbon, range), x(col.life),
  y(col.continent))




Error:
! gog: `y(continent)` maps a categorical (text) column, but `y` on `ribbon` needs a continuous (numeric) column. On these marks `x` is the domain and `y` the measure, and a category is not a quantity to measure: a mean of category names is not a number, and a region has no categorical baseline to close on. Put the category on `x` instead — `line * mean + x(<category>) + y(<number>)` is the profile plot, and `area * mean` fills it. Unlike `bar`/`box`/`interval`, these marks do not read their orientation off the bindings, because their two axes do not have the same role.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


A bare ribbon is the second refusal. A plain y() supplies one number, and a band needs two boundaries, as Why a ribbon needs a transform explained. The engine says so rather than drawing an empty panel:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_asia) + ribbon + x(year) + y(life)


data(gapminder_asia) + ribbon + x(col.year) + y(col.life)


data(gapminder_asia) + ribbon + x(:year) + y(:life)


plot(data(gapminder_asia), ribbon, x(col.year), y(col.life))




Error:
! gog: `ribbon` draws a span from a low value to a high one, but nothing here produces those extents. Add a range transform — `ribbon * range + x(t) + y(value)` draws a band between the min and max at each x, or `ribbon * bounds(lo, hi)` a pre-computed one.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


A mapped opacity is the third. Each row is one corner of a boundary, so no part of the band belongs to a single row, as One region, one fill explained. Opacity is set with style(opacity = ) and never mapped:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_asia) + ribbon * range + x(year) + y(life) + opacity(gdp)


data(gapminder_asia) + ribbon * range + x(col.year) + y(col.life) + opacity(col.gdp)


data(gapminder_asia) + ribbon * range + x(:year) + y(:life) +
  opacity(:gdp)


plot(data(gapminder_asia), layer(ribbon, range), x(col.year), y(col.life),
  opacity(col.gdp))




Error:
! gog: `opacity` cannot be bound to `ribbon` — a ribbon takes one opacity for the whole layer, not one per row. Drop the `gdp` mapping and set it with `style(opacity = )`, or use a mark that maps `opacity`.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


ribbon completes the low/high family: interval draws the pair as a whisker at each x, line and step trace its two boundaries, and ribbon fills between them. One range, four marks, which is No Exceptions made visible. See Transforms for the range, confidence and deviation statistics all four share.

title: 15  Ribbon
text:
15.14 In short
A ribbon fills a pair, and refuses to draw until a pair transform gives it one. The pair you choose is what decides the band’s meaning: the extremes from range, the middle from two quantiles, the mean’s uncertainty from confidence. Both edges are data, so the band’s shape is never a setting.

title: 15  Ribbon
text:
15.15 What comes next
A ribbon shows a region and names nothing inside it. Text draws the words: one string per row, read from a column, wherever the positions put it.




Hintze, J. L., & Nelson, R. D. (1998). Violin plots: A box plot–density trace synergism. The American Statistician, 52(2), 181–184. https://doi.org/10.1080/00031305.1998.10480559

title: 16  Text
text:
16.1 The mark and its content
Which point is which? text draws a string at each (x, y) position. It is point’s sibling: both place one glyph per row. A point’s glyph is a dot. A text mark’s glyph is a string, and that string comes from a column, through the label channel.
A point tells you where a row sits; it cannot tell you which row. Five medal counts drawn as dots are five points with nothing to say which is which:

“Given the medals: points, x is gold, y is silver.”
Bind label and draw the names themselves at those positions, and each mark now shows which row it is:
RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(medals) + text + x(gold) + y(silver) + label(country) +
  x_label("Gold") + y_label("Silver") +
  title("The same five, named")


(data(medals) + text + x(col.gold) + y(col.silver) + label(col.country) +
  x_label("Gold") + y_label("Silver") +
  title("The same five, named"))


data(medals) + text + x(:gold) + y(:silver) + label(:country) +
  x_label("Gold") + y_label("Silver") + title("The same five, named")


plot(data(medals), text, x(col.gold), y(col.silver), label(col.country),
  x_label("Gold"), y_label("Silver"), title("The same five, named"))






            USA China Great Britain Russia Germany               20 30 40   10 20 30  The same five, named Silver Gold
“Given the medals: text, x is gold, y is silver, label by country.”
That is the whole difference between the two marks. point draws the same dot at every row’s position. text draws one of the row’s own values there instead.

title: 16  Text
section: 16.2 Both at once: the labeled scatter
text:
16.2 Both at once: the labeled scatter
A dot marks one spot on the panel. A word is much wider than a dot, so a name on its own only shows roughly where its row sits. The two marks compose. Layer a point and a text over one (x, y). The dot gives the exact position and the string gives the name. That is a labeled scatter, built from two marks rather than a third mark of its own. Each style() applies to the mark written before it, so style(size = 5, color = "#9e9e9e") colors the dots and not the words. A label would otherwise sit on top of its dot, so style(nudge = "up") moves it off:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(medals) + point + style(size = 5, color = "#9e9e9e") +
  text + x(gold) + y(silver) + label(country) + style(nudge = "up") +
  x_label("Gold") + y_label("Silver") +
  title("Located by the dot, named just above")


(data(medals) + point + style(size = 5, color = "#9e9e9e") +
  text + x(col.gold) + y(col.silver) + label(col.country) + style(nudge = "up") +
  x_label("Gold") + y_label("Silver") +
  title("Located by the dot, named just above"))


data(medals) + point + style(size = 5, color = "#9e9e9e") + text +
  x(:gold) + y(:silver) + label(:country) + style(nudge = "up") +
  x_label("Gold") + y_label("Silver") +
  title("Located by the dot, named just above")


plot(data(medals), point, style({ size: 5, color: "#9e9e9e" }), text,
  x(col.gold), y(col.silver), label(col.country), style({ nudge: "up" }),
  x_label("Gold"), y_label("Silver"),
  title("Located by the dot, named just above"))






                   USA China Great Britain Russia Germany               20 30 40   10 20 30  Located by the dot, named just above Silver Gold





“Given the medals: points and also text, x is gold, y is silver, label by country, with nudge up.”
There is no “labeled point” mark to learn: a labeled scatter is just point + text, layered with the + operator.
Five names fit here. Fifty would not, and choosing which few to keep is the hardest part of a labeled scatter. A plot that carries brush() lets you try a few in the web edition before you write any down. Clicking a mark there prints its values on the plot, which Selection calls a stamp. A stamp disappears when the page reloads. A text label is part of the specification, so it is drawn every time.

16.2.1 Nudging the label off its point
Up is only one of four directions, and it is not always the side with room. A dot near the top of the panel, or one with a neighbor just above it, has no space for its name there. Those labels need a different direction. style(nudge = ) shifts a text label off its (x, y). It takes one direction: "up", "down", "left", or "right":


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(medals) + point + style(size = 5, color = "#9e9e9e") +
  text + x(gold) + y(silver) + label(country) + style(nudge = "right") +
  x_label("Gold") + y_label("Silver") +
  title("The same, nudged right")


(data(medals) + point + style(size = 5, color = "#9e9e9e") +
  text + x(col.gold) + y(col.silver) + label(col.country) + style(nudge = "right") +
  x_label("Gold") + y_label("Silver") +
  title("The same, nudged right"))


data(medals) + point + style(size = 5, color = "#9e9e9e") + text +
  x(:gold) + y(:silver) + label(:country) + style(nudge = "right") +
  x_label("Gold") + y_label("Silver") + title("The same, nudged right")


plot(data(medals), point, style({ size: 5, color: "#9e9e9e" }), text,
  x(col.gold), y(col.silver), label(col.country),
  style({ nudge: "right" }), x_label("Gold"), y_label("Silver"),
  title("The same, nudged right"))






                   USA China Great Britain Russia Germany               20 30 40   10 20 30  The same, nudged right Silver Gold





You do not give a distance. The engine takes it from the font size, far enough to clear a default dot, so nudge asks only for a direction. A nudge is one fixed shift, the same for every label, and nothing in the data changes it. jitter and dodge work the other way: they compute their offsets from the data, so every mark moves by its own amount. Only text accepts a nudge. A point or a bar has no label to move, so the engine refuses the setting there and names the mark that does.


16.2.2 repel: moving labels off each other
A nudge shifts every label the same way, so it moves each label off its own dot and does nothing else. When the labels collide with each other, one fixed shift moves them all together and the words still overlap. Thirty European countries are enough to show it:

repel solves that, and it is a collision modifier rather than a setting. It measures where the labels and the dots actually are, then moves each label off the words around it:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript

  text * repel + x(gdp) + y(life) + label(country) +

  x(:gdp) + y(:life) + label(:country) + x_label("GDP per capita") +
  y_label("Life expectancy") + title("The same thirty, moved apart")


plot(data(gm_europe), point, style({ color: "#9e9e9e" }),
  layer(text, repel), x(col.gdp), y(col.life), label(col.country),
  x_label("GDP per capita"), y_label("Life expectancy"),
  title("The same thirty, moved apart"))






                                                 Albania Austria Belgium Bosnia and Herzegovina Bulgaria Croatia Czech Republic Denmark Finland France Germany Greece Hungary Iceland Ireland Italy Montenegro Netherlands Norway Poland Portugal Romania Serbia Slovak Republic Slovenia Spain Sweden Switzerland Turkey United Kingdom                    10K 20K 30K 40K 50K   72 74 76 78 80 82  The same thirty, moved apart Life expectancy GDP per capita





“Given gapminder Europe: points and also text derived by repel, x is gdp, y is life, label by country.”
Three things in that picture are worth naming. Every label comes to rest just outside its dot, so no word covers the point it names. A label in a crowd slides to whichever side has room. A label with space around it stays directly above its dot. All three follow from one rule: repel pulls a label toward its own dot and pushes it away from every word and every other dot.
A label sometimes has to travel much further than any of these did. Once it ends up more than one line of text from its point, gog draws a thin line from the point to the word. That line is what tells you which point the name belongs to. None of the thirty labels moves that far, so repel draws no line here.
The placement is deterministic. It uses no random-number generator and no system time, so the same specification draws the same picture every time.
When no arrangement fits, repel still draws every label and reports how many still overlap. It never drops a label without saying so. A plot missing the names it could not fit would look like a plot of fewer countries, so gog reports the count instead. Thirty countries all fit, so no report appears here. Three things give crowded labels more room: fewer rows, a smaller style(size = ), and a larger plot. theme(width =, height =) sets the plot’s size in pixels, and the Composition chapter covers it.
The setting and the collision modifier compose, and each does one thing. style(nudge = ) says which side a label prefers, and repel resolves the overlaps that remain:

  title("Nudged right first, then moved apart")

  text * repel + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) + label(col.country) + style(nudge = "right") +
  x_label("GDP per capita") + y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("Nudged right first, then moved apart"))


data(gm_europe) + point + style(color = "#9e9e9e") + text * repel +
  x(:gdp) + y(:life) + label(:country) + style(nudge = "right") +
  x_label("GDP per capita") + y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("Nudged right first, then moved apart")


plot(data(gm_europe), point, style({ color: "#9e9e9e" }),
  layer(text, repel), x(col.gdp), y(col.life), label(col.country),
  style({ nudge: "right" }), x_label("GDP per capita"),
  y_label("Life expectancy"),
  title("Nudged right first, then moved apart"))

title: 16  Text
section: 16.3 Numeric labels: the value on each mark
text:
16.3 Numeric labels: the value on each mark
A label does not have to be a name, and it does not have to sit on a scatter. A bar shows which country won more. To read by how much, a reader has to measure each bar against the axis, and that is an estimate. Sometimes the number itself is the answer. Bind a column that holds numbers and each row’s value is drawn. A whole number is printed without a decimal point. Layer text over bar to print each bar’s height at its top:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(medals) + bar + style(color = "steelblue") +
  text + x(country) + y(gold) + label(gold) +
  y_label("Gold medals") +
  title("Each bar labeled with its height")


(data(medals) + bar + style(color = "steelblue") +
  text + x(col.country) + y(col.gold) + label(col.gold) +
  y_label("Gold medals") +
  title("Each bar labeled with its height"))


data(medals) + bar + style(color = "steelblue") + text + x(:country) +
  y(:gold) + label(:gold) + y_label("Gold medals") +
  title("Each bar labeled with its height")


plot(data(medals), bar, style({ color: "steelblue" }), text,
  x(col.country), y(col.gold), label(col.gold), y_label("Gold medals"),
  title("Each bar labeled with its height"))






                  46 38 29 19 17                   USA China Great Britain Russia Germany   0 10 20 30 40  Each bar labeled with its height Gold medals Country

By default every label is printed in one color. You see a hue faster than you can read a word. A color split therefore shows the grouping before the name. title: 16  Text
text:
16.5 Styling: one color, one size
A color channel takes its hues from a column. A color you choose yourself is a different thing: a setting rather than a mapping. When the labels are the plot rather than notes beside it, the default font is often too small to read comfortably. A larger size is a setting too. Neither comes from a column, and that is what makes them settings. style(color = ) sets the color of the words. style(size = ) sets the font size in pixels. Each applies to every label in the layer:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(medals) + text + x(gold) + y(silver) + label(country) +
  style(color = "seagreen", size = 17) +
  x_label("Gold") + y_label("Silver") +
  title("Bigger, greener labels")


(data(medals) + text + x(col.gold) + y(col.silver) + label(col.country) +
  style(color = "seagreen", size = 17) +
  x_label("Gold") + y_label("Silver") +
  title("Bigger, greener labels"))


data(medals) + text + x(:gold) + y(:silver) + label(:country) +
  style(color = "seagreen", size = 17) + x_label("Gold") +
  y_label("Silver") + title("Bigger, greener labels")


plot(data(medals), text, x(col.gold), y(col.silver), label(col.country),
  style({ color: "seagreen", size: 17 }), x_label("Gold"),
  y_label("Silver"), title("Bigger, greener labels"))

“Given the medals: text, x is gold, y is silver, label by country, colored seagreen, with size 17.”
style(size = ) gives every label in the layer one font size. A word cloud is the plot this rules out. It sizes each word by its frequency, so it needs a size per row. What you can set shows what the engine answers when you ask for one.

title: 16  Text
text:
16.6 Why label is a channel
A setting is a value you type into the sentence. You might expect a label to work the same way, the way a title is typed. A label is not a title: it is one value per row, and that makes it data. text requires a label: it is the mark’s minimum syllable, the way x and y are. Ask for a text mark with no label and the engine refuses, and says what to write instead, as What it refuses shows.
The grammar’s own rule decides this. A label’s string is data, and data reaches a mark only through a channel. That makes label a channel, so no mark takes the words themselves as an argument. A fixed note is therefore a table with one row, handed to data(), and never a value handed to style(). Only text accepts label; every other mark refuses it, which is why a labeled scatter is point + text and never a label on point. text is the mark, and label is the channel that carries the column it draws.

If you have used ggplot2, a note there is a separate function, annotate(). In gog it is a table with one row, and that table is worth seeing drawn. A second data() opens a second layer over its own table (the Data chapter’s rule), and a table with one row in it puts one string on the plot:

Nothing was added to the grammar to reach that. data() already binds the nearest table, text already draws one string per row, and a note is simply a table with one row in it. The note is data like any other, so it is scaled like any other. Give it an x far from the points and the axes stretch to cover it, which is worth checking before you settle on a position.
One rule applies while writing a note. x and y belong to the whole plot, so the note’s table needs a column for each. The income_note table reuses the plot’s own column names, gdp and life. A note with its own names writes its positions after text: + text + x(at) + y(value) + label(what). Anything else annotate() places by data values can be written this way too. A dot on the plot is a point over the same one-row table, and several notes are several rows.

title: 16  Text
text:
16.8 Text that a transform places
A note names a place you chose. A transform can choose the place instead, and then the text names whatever that transform built. Each of these sentences has a sibling that draws the shape the text is labeling:



Text derived by
What it labels




text * layout
the nodes of a network, beside point * layout and edge * layout


text * flow
the blocks of a flow, beside ribbon * flow and zone * flow


text * partition
the boxes of a packing, beside zone * partition


text * repel
the scatter labels of repel, moved apart until they fit



The chapters that draw them are Network, Flow and Transforms. In each one the text is a layer over the mark that drew the shape, and both layers read the same transform.

title: 16  Text
text:
16.9 What you can set
The Styling section set a color and a size. Those are two entries in a longer list, and the rest of it is here: which size, which color, and which side of the dot. None of that is in a column, so it is set rather than mapped, and each mark takes its own settings. These are a text mark’s, with the values each accepts:



Setting
Value

style(opacity = )

style(size = )
pixels


style(nudge = )
up, down, left, right

title: 16  Text

16.10 What it refuses
A text with no label is refused first. The label is the mark’s minimum syllable, the way x and y are, for the reason Why label is a channel gave. The engine refuses and names the channel to add:

A reader who knows point will try its channels on text, and one of them cannot do anything to a string. A point’s glyph can change shape because the dot itself says nothing. A text mark’s glyph is the word, so there is nothing for shape to change:
