If the two series are genuinely in different units, facet on the measure instead.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


A second scale on one axis is a second axis. One panel would then hold two coordinate spaces, and every mark would be placed by an axis that no sentence in the plot names. This refusal and the milestones plot differ by one argument: a layer names its own column, never its own scale.

title: 27  Encoding scope
section: 27.3 Channels: plot-scoped or layer-scoped, by position
text:
27.3 Channels: plot-scoped or layer-scoped, by position
Positions had to share one axis, which is why they needed a section of their own. The other channels have no shared axis between layers. They follow the same position rule.
A channel is often meant for one layer alone. You may want the points colored by group and one plain line drawn through them. Written after a mark, a channel binds to that mark alone:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + x(gdp) + y(life) +
  point + color(continent) +   # color applies to point only
  line                         # line uses a single default color


(data(gapminder_2007) + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) +
  point + color(col.continent) +
  line)


data(gapminder_2007) + x(:gdp) + y(:life) + point + color(:continent) +
  line


plot(data(gapminder_2007), x(col.gdp), y(col.life), point,
  color(col.continent), line)






                                                                                                                                                                                     0K 10K 20K 30K 40K 50K   40 50 60 70 80  Life Gdp  Continent    Asia  Europe  Africa  Americas  Oceania 





“Given gapminder 2007: x is gdp, y is life, points colored by continent, and also a line.”
Written before any mark, a channel has no mark to bind to. It binds to the plot instead, so every layer gets it:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + x(gdp) + y(life) + color(continent) +
  point +
  line


(data(gapminder_2007) + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) + color(col.continent) +
  point +
  line)


data(gapminder_2007) + x(:gdp) + y(:life) + color(:continent) + point +
  line


plot(data(gapminder_2007), x(col.gdp), y(col.life), color(col.continent),
  point, line)

title: 27  Encoding scope
text:
27.5 What comes next
Scope decides which layer reads an atom inside one panel. Faceting makes more panels, one per category of a column. Every panel is drawn by the same sentence and read against the same axes.

title: 28  Faceting
text:
28.1 |: panels side by side
How do you compare the same plot across groups? A facet splits one plot into small multiples: one panel per category of a column. Wilkinson calls a facet a frame of frames. A frame is the space a plot is drawn in, with its own x and y axes. The facet column’s categories make the outer frame. Every cell of that outer frame holds one copy of the inner frame, which is the plot itself. Nothing else about the plot changes. The marks, channels, and transforms you have already learned draw each panel exactly as they would draw one plot with no facet.
The picture has been invented more than once, so you may know it under another name. Becker and Cleveland’s group at Bell Labs built it into S as Trellis display (Becker et al., 1996). The name comes from the garden trellis, because the panels are arranged in rows and columns like one. Most people first met the display in S-PLUS. R draws it that way still in the lattice package (Sarkar, 2026), and its own book is where the display is set out in full (Sarkar, 2008). Base R’s coplot() is the same idea under a third name, the conditioning plot, because what a trellis conditions on is the facet column. That is also why the operator in the next section is |, the sign that statistics already uses for conditioning. Composition finishes that history.
Tufte’s small multiples (Tufte, 1990) names the result rather than the operation, which is the division this book keeps: small multiples for the picture, facet for the thing you write.
Facet is Wilkinson’s own word (Wilkinson, 2005), from the Latin facies, a face: one side of a many-sided thing, like one face of a cut diamond. gog takes Wilkinson’s word because it is the most general of them. To him a trellis is one arrangement a facet can take, beside the scatterplot matrix and the row plot. A grammar needs one term that covers all three. The word every one of these systems shares is panel, the cell a split produces, and this chapter uses it the same way.
The scatter of income against life expectancy holds five continents in one cloud. You want to see each on its own without losing the comparison between them. The facet() atom names the column that does the splitting, and | arranges the panels in columns:

“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp, y is life, split into panel columns by continent.”
Reading across, the panels share both axes, so a shift between continents reads as plainly as a pattern within one. The shared scale is what faceting is for. One plot per continent, each with its own scale, looks almost the same on the page. It breaks the comparison, and nothing warns the reader.

title: 28  Faceting
text:
28.2 /: panels stacked
Are lives in Africa shorter than in Europe, and by how much? That is a question about where each distribution sits along one axis. / arranges the panels in rows. Stacking the panels aligns their x axes. That is the arrangement to choose when the question is where the values sit along x:

gm_ae <- gapminder_2007[gapminder_2007$continent %in% c("Africa", "Americas", "Europe"), ]
data(gm_ae) + bar * bin + x(life) / facet(continent)



                              0 5 10 15                                    0 5 10 15                                   50 60 70 80   0 5 10 15    Europe  Africa  Americas  Count Life





“Given the gm ae table: bars derived by bin, x is life, split into panel rows by continent.”
Each panel’s bars sit directly above the bars covering the same span of life expectancy in the panel below. Africa’s life expectancies spread wide toward the low end, Europe’s cluster in a narrow band at the high end, and the Americas sit between the two.
That reading only works because the bars are the same width in all three panels. A histogram under a facet needs two separate decisions: where the bins are cut, and which rows are counted in them. Each panel counts its own rows, because a statistic is computed on the panel’s subset as if that subset were the whole table. That is true of every transform on every mark, which is the No Exceptions law applied one panel at a time.
But bin is not only a statistic. It cuts the axis into cells and counts the rows in each one. The cut describes the axis rather than measuring the rows, so it belongs with the shared scale. One set of bins is cut from all three panels’ rows at once, and each panel then counts only its own rows into those bins.
It is worth seeing what the other choice would draw. Suppose each panel cut its own bins. Europe’s narrow spread would get narrow bins and Africa’s wide spread would get wide ones, so bars of different widths would be drawn against a single axis. A bar four years wide holding nine countries and a bar one year wide holding eight then draw at nearly the same height. The first holds about two countries per year and the second holds eight, so the two rates differ by more than three times. The panels are still aligned and the axis still looks correct, and yet a reader cannot compare the three distributions.

title: 28  Faceting
text:
28.3 Crossing into a grid
Every plot so far has split on one column. Two columns can matter at once. Here the question is how each continent’s countries moved between 1957 and 2007, which is a split by continent and by period together. Write both operators to cross two columns into a grid. Each operator applies to the facet written after it, read left to right:

gm_years <- gm_all[gm_all$year %in% c(1957, 2007), ]
gm_years$period <- as.character(gm_years$year)
data(gm_years) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) | facet(continent) / facet(period)



                                                          40 60 80                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 0K 50K 100K   40 60 80                                                      0K 50K 100K                                                                              0K 50K 100K                                                   0K 50K 100K                            0K 50K 100K      Asia  Europe  Africa  Americas  Oceania    1957  2007  Life Gdp





“Given the gm years table: points, x is gdp, y is life, split into panel columns by continent and panel rows by period.”
Fifty years and five continents in one grid: every panel column is a continent, and every panel row a period. The shared scale lets you measure the rise in life expectancy panel by panel.
The grid is a crossing in Wilkinson’s sense: every combination of a panel column and a panel row gets a panel, and a combination with no matching rows still gets an empty one. The grid shows that the combination is possible, so an empty panel is information rather than an accident. Wilkinson’s other operation, nesting, draws only the combinations that exist. gog’s facet operators always cross, so every combination gets a panel. Neither is gog’s nest() atom, which packs a whole into areas.

section: 28.4 Folding a long line of panels
text:
28.4 Folding a long line of panels
Back on one column, the opposite trouble appears. One column with many categories makes a long line of panels, and a long line of panels makes each one narrow. Here are the ten most populous countries of 2007. Each panel shows one country’s life expectancy from 1952 to 2007:

ranked <- gapminder_2007[base::order(-gapminder_2007$population), ]
gm_top <- gm_all[gm_all$country %in% utils::head(ranked$country, 10), ]
data(gm_top) + line + group(country) + x(year) + y(life) | facet(country)



                               1960 1980 2000   40 50 60 70 80                           1960 1980 2000                             1960 1980 2000                             1960 1980 2000                             1960 1980 2000                             1960 1980 2000                             1960 1980 2000                             1960 1980 2000                             1960 1980 2000                             1960 1980 2000      Bangladesh  Brazil  China  India  Indonesia  Japan  Mexico  Nigeria  Pakistan  United States  Life Year





“Given the gm top table: lines, x is year, y is life, grouped by country, split into panel columns by country.”
The shapes are still readable. Nothing else on the panel can be read. Look at the axis: the tick labels touch and print as one run of digits, 196019802000, and the last panel’s name is wider than the strip that prints it. Ten categories is a common number, and ten panels in one line are already too narrow to read.
wrap folds that line into a rectangle. The number is how many panels to draw before the line begins again:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gm_top) + line + group(country) + x(year) + y(life) | facet(country, wrap = 4)


data(gm_top) + line + group(col.country) + x(col.year) + y(col.life) | facet(col.country, wrap = 4)


data(gm_top) + line + group(:country) + x(:year) + y(:life) |
  facet(:country, wrap = 4)


plot(data(gm_top), line, group(col.country), x(col.year), y(col.life),
  across(col.country, { wrap: 4 }))






                              40 50 60 70 80                                                                                                          40 50 60 70 80                                                    1960 1980 2000                             1960 1980 2000                                  1960 1980 2000   40 50 60 70 80                           1960 1980 2000      Bangladesh  Brazil  China  India  Indonesia  Japan  Mexico  Nigeria  Pakistan  United States  Life Year





“Given the gm top table: lines, x is year, y is life, grouped by country, split into panel columns by country, wrapped at 4.”
The panels, the scale and the sentence are unchanged, and wrap = 4 is the only addition. The years are readable, United States fits its strip, and each country’s rise is now large enough to read.
Notice what wrap does not say: which way the panels run. The operator already decides it. | runs the line across, so four to a row; / runs it down, so four to a column:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gm_top) + line + group(country) + x(year) + y(life) / facet(country, wrap = 4)


data(gm_top) + line + group(col.country) + x(col.year) + y(col.life) / facet(col.country, wrap = 4)


data(gm_top) + line + group(:country) + x(:year) + y(:life) /
  facet(:country, wrap = 4)


plot(data(gm_top), line, group(col.country), x(col.year), y(col.life),
  down(col.country, { wrap: 4 }))






                              40 50 60 70 80                                                                                 40 50 60 70 80                                                    1960 1980 2000                                 40 50 60 70 80                                                         1960 1980 2000   40 50 60 70 80                           1960 1980 2000      Bangladesh  Indonesia  Pakistan  Brazil  Japan  United States  China  Mexico  India  Nigeria  Life Year





The same number, the same ten countries, read down the columns instead of across the rows. One number is enough because the direction is already in the sentence, which is why facet() takes no second argument for it. ggplot2 spells the same idea as nrow and ncol.
Two details in the wrapped plots come from the fold itself. The first is the bottom right, where the last row stops after two panels. Ten panels folded four to a row fill twelve cells, so two cells are left over and nothing is drawn in them. They are not the empty panels of the previous section. In a crossing, an empty panel stands for a combination the frame allows, and its emptiness reports that the table holds no rows for it. Here there is no combination at all, only leftover space.
The second is the extra axis beside the gap. Tick labels belong to the panels that touch the edge where the axis is drawn. In a full rectangle that edge is the bottom row. A folded line can leave the last row short, and then that rule stops describing the plot. So gog uses a more general rule: a panel draws the x axis when no panel sits below it. In the plot folded with |, Mexico and Nigeria sit above the gap and keep their year labels. In the one folded with /, the gap falls under United States.
Wrapping a crossed grid is refused. The crossing already makes a rectangle from two columns, so a panel count beside it would answer the same question a second time:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gm_years) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) |
  facet(continent, wrap = 2) / facet(period)


(data(gm_years) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) |
  facet(col.continent, wrap = 2) / facet(col.period))


data(gm_years) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life) |
  facet(:continent, wrap = 2) / facet(:period)


plot(data(gm_years), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life),
  across(col.continent, { wrap: 2 }), down(col.period))




Error:
! gog: `wrap` folds one line of panels into a rectangle, but `continent` and `period` already cross into one. Drop `wrap`, or facet by one column and let `wrap` shape it.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


A crossed grid already takes its shape from the two columns, so there is no line left to fold.

“Given all the gapminder years: a line derived by sum, x is year, y is population, split into panel columns by continent, wrapped at 3.”
Asia is nearly four billion people and Oceania about twenty-five million, so the axis is sized for Asia and Oceania is a flat line along the bottom. Oceania’s line is drawn correctly, but the axis is too tall for its shape to show. The plot is correct. It shows that these five quantities are of very different sizes. But the question was how each continent grew, and the plot answers a different one.
Write free = TRUE inside a position, and that position’s axis is fitted to each panel’s own rows:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gm_all) + line * sum + x(year) +
  y(population, free = TRUE) | facet(continent, wrap = 3)


(data(gm_all) + line * sum + x(col.year) +
  y(col.population, free = True) | facet(col.continent, wrap = 3))


data(gm_all) + line * sum + x(:year) + y(:population, free = true) |
  facet(:continent, wrap = 3)


plot(data(gm_all), layer(line, sum), x(col.year),
  y(col.population, { free: true }), across(col.continent, { wrap: 3 }))

“Given all the gapminder years: a line derived by sum, x is year, y is population, freed, split into panel columns by continent, wrapped at 3.”
Now every panel has a shape, and Oceania has more than doubled. Notice the y axis: each panel carries its own numbers, because one set of labels along the edge is enough only when the scale is shared.
Notice also what the second plot loses. All five panels now look alike: five lines rising left to right at about the same angle. Set the five panels side by side, and nothing in them shows that one climb is measured in billions and another in tens of millions. A reader who looks at the shapes and not at the axes will draw the wrong conclusion. The first plot cannot mislead a reader this way; the second one can. So gog frees a scale only when you ask for it.
Which axis is freed is decided by where you write it. You write free inside x() or inside y(), so the sentence has already named the axis and free does not name it again. There is no free_x or free_y, and freeing both is writing it twice:

  facet(continent, wrap = 3)

  facet(col.continent, wrap = 3))


data(gm_all) + point + x(:gdp, free = true) + y(:life, free = true) |
  facet(:continent, wrap = 3)


plot(data(gm_all), point, x(col.gdp, { free: true }),
  y(col.life, { free: true }), across(col.continent, { wrap: 3 }))

There is a third position, and it takes free the same way. A cube sits in a panel like any other plot (Space):


RPythonJuliaJavaScript

  z(population, free = TRUE) + color(continent) | facet(continent)


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) +
  z(col.population, free = True) + color(col.continent) | facet(col.continent))

  z(:population, free = true) + color(:continent) | facet(:continent)


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life),
  z(col.population, { free: true }), color(col.continent),
  across(col.continent))

“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp, y is life, z is population, freed, color by continent, split into panel columns by continent.”
If the height axis were shared, it would have to reach China, and Oceania’s two countries would sit at the very bottom, too close together to read. Freed, Oceania is measured in tens of millions and has a shape again. The loss is the one described above: the five cubes can no longer be compared with each other. That plot needs no new word in the grammar. free is written on a position and z is a position, so the third one accepts it like the other two.
Freeing any of the three positions has two further effects and one limit. gog applies all three, and none is a setting you can write. The first is the bin cut. The histogram earlier in this chapter shares one set of bin edges across every panel, because a cut describes the axis and the axis was shared. Free the axis and the edges are cut per panel too, for exactly the same reason:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gm_all) + bar * bin + x(gdp, free = TRUE) | facet(continent, wrap = 3)


data(gm_all) + bar * bin + x(col.gdp, free = True) | facet(col.continent, wrap = 3)


data(gm_all) + bar * bin + x(:gdp, free = true) |
  facet(:continent, wrap = 3)


plot(data(gm_all), layer(bar, bin), x(col.gdp, { free: true }),
  across(col.continent, { wrap: 3 }))






                                  50K 100K   0 100 200 300 400                                      10K 20K 30K 40K                                       5K 10K 15K 20K                                             10K 20K 30K 40K   0 100 200 300 400                             20K 30K      Asia  Europe  Africa  Americas  Oceania  Count Gdp





Each panel is cut from its own rows, so Africa gets bins the size of Africa’s spread rather than bins sized for the richest countries in the data. You cannot combine a free scale with a shared cut. Each panel would count only its own rows, while the bin edges came from every panel’s rows together, so the bars would not fit the axis under them.
The second is the panel’s guides: its axis numbers and gridlines. A scale decides where the marks go and where the axis prints its numbers. Freeing the scale has to move both, or the numbers stop describing the picture. Look again at the plot where y(population, free = TRUE) was written. Its gridlines sit at different heights in every panel, and each panel’s labels sit beside its own. When the scale is shared, those same lines are drawn at one set of heights across all five. That is what a freed guide means: the lines a reader reads values from belong to the scale that was freed.
The third is that a free scale belongs to a panel, never to an animation frame. play (Play) splits rows the same way a facet does, so free on a played plot looks like the same request. gog refuses it:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gm_all) + point + x(gdp) + y(life, free = TRUE) + play(year)


data(gm_all) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life, free = True) + play(col.year)


data(gm_all) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life, free = true) + play(:year)


plot(data(gm_all), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life, { free: true }),
  play(col.year))




Error:
! gog: `y(life, free = TRUE)` fits one scale per *panel*, and this plot has frames rather than panels. A frame replaces the one before it, so an axis refitted per frame would move under the data and the motion would be the scale's rather than the data's. Facet the plot to free a scale across panels, or leave the sequence on one scale.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


The reason is in the message. Panels sit beside each other and a reader compares them. A frame replaces the frame before it, so a refitted axis would show different numbers in every frame. The reader would then see movement that comes from the changing axis rather than from the data. Across panels a free scale is safe. Across frames it would misreport the data.
Two more sentences are refused for the same kind of reason. Only x, y and z take free, because a channel that is not a position has no axis to free, only a legend, and that one legend decodes the whole plot. And with no facet there are no panels:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life, free = TRUE)


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life, free = True)


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life, free = true)


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life, { free: true }))




Error:
! gog: `y(life, free = TRUE)` fits one scale per panel, and this plot has one panel. Facet it — `plot | facet(<column>)` — or drop `free`.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


Both messages name what is missing: an axis to free, or panels to free it in.

title: 28  Faceting
section: 28.6 A layer without the facet column
text:
28.6 A layer without the facet column
Five panels are easier to compare when every one of them carries the same reference line, such as the world’s median life expectancy. A layer whose table does not have the facet column is drawn in full in every panel. That is how one shared reference line is drawn behind small multiples:

data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) +
  data(world_median) + line + style(color = "gray", size = 1) |
  facet(continent)


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) +
  data(world_median) + line + style(color = "gray", size = 1) |
  facet(col.continent))


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life) + data(world_median) +
  line + style(color = "gray", size = 1) | facet(:continent)


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life),
  data(world_median), line, style({ color: "gray", size: 1 }),
  across(col.continent))




gog: table `world_median` has no column `continent`, so its layer is drawn in every panel. If it should be split too, add `continent` to that table.




                                                                        0K 10K 20K 30K 40K 50K   40 50 60 70 80                                                                 0K 10K 20K 30K 40K 50K                                                                                         0K 10K 20K 30K 40K 50K                                                              0K 10K 20K 30K 40K 50K                                       0K 10K 20K 30K 40K 50K      Asia  Europe  Africa  Americas  Oceania  Life Gdp





“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp, y is life, and also a line from the world median, split into panel columns by continent.”
The gray line, the world’s median life expectancy, repeats in every panel, so each continent is read against the same line. The engine reports this as an assumption rather than doing it in silence: the table world_median has no continent column, so its layer is drawn everywhere.

title: 28  Faceting
text:
28.7 The facet column’s type
You may want one panel for small countries and one for large ones, which is a split by population. A facet column names the panels, so it must be a categorical column: a number is a position along an axis, not a name for a frame. Faceting by a continuous column refuses with direction:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) | facet(population)


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) | facet(col.population)


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life) | facet(:population)


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life),
  across(col.population))




Error:
! gog: `facet(population)` splits on a number column, but a facet variable names the panels, so it must be a category column. Make `population` text — in R, `factor(population)` — or cut it into named groups first.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


shape and group need a categorical column too, because each of them names groups rather than measures them. A facet asks the same of the column that names its panels. Turn the column into text, or cut it into named groups, and the names you choose are the panels you get. In R that is factor() or cut().
Trellis named that cut a shingle, and lattice still builds one with shingle() or equal.count(). A shingle’s intervals are allowed to overlap, so one row can appear in two panels. That makes the change from panel to panel smoother, and it counts some rows twice. The cut you write yourself loses that smoothing, and in exchange it prints its boundaries in the strip labels, where a reader can check them.
Faceting joins with the operators, never with +; a facet is a property of the whole plot’s frame, not one more encoding in the chain. Write + facet(continent) and gog refuses, and the message points you at | and /.

title: 28  Faceting
text:
28.8 In short
Every panel is drawn by the same sentence and read against the same scales. | puts the panels in columns, / puts them in rows, and writing both crosses two columns into a grid. wrap folds one long line into a rectangle, and free releases the shared scale so each panel is fitted to its own rows. A layer whose table does not carry the facet column is drawn in full in every panel.

title: 28  Faceting
text:
28.9 What comes next
Faceting cuts one plot into panels that share a sentence and both of their axes. Composition does the opposite: it arranges plots that were never one plot on a single page.

title: 29  Composition
text:
29.1 Two plots, one page
How do you put two different plots on one page? Faceting splits one plot into panels. Composition does the opposite: it takes plots that were never one plot and arranges them on a page. Wilkinson separates the two, noting that “some tabled graphics are really two or more graphics glued together”. gog separates them too, with the operators you have already learned. | places two things side by side, and / places one above the other, whether those things are panels or whole plots:
A facet splits one plot by a column of its data. A page arranges finished plots, and says nothing about any plot’s data. What you write on the right of the operator decides which one you get, and nothing else does.
Two views of one table often belong side by side, even when they share no axis. Write each plot in full, then put | between them:

  (data(gapminder_2007) + bar * count + x(continent) + theme(tick_angle = 45))

  (data(gapminder_2007) + bar * count + x(col.continent) + theme(tick_angle = 45)))

  theme(tick_angle = 45))


beside(plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life)),
  plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(bar, count), x(col.continent),
  theme({ tick_angle: 45 })))






                                                                                                                                                                                    0K 10K 20K 30K 40K 50K   40 50 60 70 80  Life Gdp


                              Asia Europe Africa Americas Oceania   0 20 40  Count Continent
“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp, y is life, beside bars derived by count, x is continent.”
The two plots measure entirely different things: a country’s income against its life expectancy, and how many countries each continent holds. They share nothing, not a scale, not an axis, not a legend, because there is nothing to share. The page divides evenly between them, so each plot keeps half the width. That is why the bar plot turns its continent names with theme(tick_angle = 45).
/ places the same two plots one above the other. Each one now has the full width of the page, so the continent names fit without turning:
RPythonJuliaJavaScript


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life)) /
  (data(gapminder_2007) + bar * count + x(continent))


((data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life)) /
  (data(gapminder_2007) + bar * count + x(col.continent)))


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life)) /
  (data(gapminder_2007) + bar * count + x(:continent))


below(plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life)),
  plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(bar, count), x(col.continent)))






                                                                                                                                                                                    0K 10K 20K 30K 40K 50K   40 50 60 70 80  Life Gdp


                              Asia Europe Africa Americas Oceania   0 20 40  Count Continent
“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp, y is life, above bars derived by count, x is continent.”
Both operators take pages as well as plots, so a page can hold another page. (a | b) / c is a row of two plots above a third, and the marginal plot later in this chapter is built that way.
In R, Python and Julia, / is applied before |, so a | b / c reads as a | (b / c). Add parentheses whenever the order changes the picture. JavaScript spells the operators as words, so there is no order to remember. The JavaScript chapter shows those words.

title: 29  Composition
section: 29.2 A shared column is a shared axis
text:
29.2 A shared column is a shared axis
The two plots in that figure share no column. One shared column changes what the page draws. Two composed plots stay unrelated until both name the same column on the same axis. The arrangement decides which axis: x when one plot is above the other, and y when the two sit side by side. When both name it, that is not two axes that happen to look alike; it is one axis, and gog treats it as one:

The same column on the aligned axis of two composed plots is one axis: one scale, one panel extent, drawn once.

Here are two plots, both reading gdp on x. The theme(height = 150) on the first asks for 150 pixels of the page’s height:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


(data(gapminder_2007) + bar * bin + x(gdp) + theme(height = 150)) /
  (data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life))


((data(gapminder_2007) + bar * bin + x(col.gdp) + theme(height = 150)) /
  (data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life)))


(data(gapminder_2007) + bar * bin + x(:gdp) + theme(height = 150)) /
  (data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life))


below(plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(bar, bin), x(col.gdp),
  theme({ height: 150 })),
  plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life)))






                                      0 20 40 60  Count


                                                                                                                                                                            0K 20K 40K   40 50 60 70 80  Life Gdp






“Given gapminder 2007: bars derived by bin, x is gdp, above points, x is gdp, y is life.”
Look at what the rule did. The histogram’s panel is exactly as wide as the scatter’s, so each bar is drawn directly above the points it counts. Both plots measure gdp over the same range, so equal distances across the two panels stand for equal amounts of gdp. And the gdp axis is written once, along the bottom, because there is only one axis to write. Faceting makes the same decision when it puts tick labels only under the bottom row of panels.
A plot that draws no axis reserves no margin for one. That is why the histogram sits close to the scatter, with no strip of tick labels between the two panels.

29.2.1 One axis, but not one legend
Having seen an axis merge, you might expect a shared legend to merge the same way. Compose two plots that both map color and you get two legends, one for each:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) + color(continent)) |
  (data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(population) + y(life) + color(continent))


((data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) + color(col.continent)) |
  (data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.population) + y(col.life) + color(col.continent)))


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life) + color(:continent)) |
  (data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:population) + y(:life) +
  color(:continent))


beside(plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life),
  color(col.continent)),
  plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.population), y(col.life),
  color(col.continent)))






                                                                                                                                                                                    0K 10K 20K 30K 40K 50K   40 50 60 70 80  Life Gdp  Continent    Asia  Europe  Africa  Americas  Oceania 


                                                                                                                                                                       0M 500M 1000M    Population  Continent    Asia  Europe  Africa  Americas  Oceania 






“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp, y is life, color by continent, beside points, x is population, y is life, color by continent.”
Look at what that figure draws once, and what it draws twice. Both plots read life on y, so that axis is shared and written a single time, on the left. Both color by continent as well, and there you get two legends, saying exactly the same thing.
Axes merge and legends do not, and that difference is deliberate. Axes merge because there is an exact test: the same column on the same axis means one scale must be right for both plots. A legend has no such test. These two plots do agree, because both split by continent. But nothing in the grammar makes any two composed plots agree. The next pair may split by different columns, or map one column onto two scales. One legend over those two would be wrong for one of them. Nothing in the picture shows the error, because it still looks like a legend.
So gog merges no legend. Two identical legends side by side tell you that the two plots split by the same column.
When you want one legend over several panels, use faceting instead. A facet is one plot split by a column, so every panel is colored by the same scale. It draws a single legend. The choice between | and facet() is the choice between two plots and one.

title: 29  Composition
text:
29.3 The marginal plot
The histogram sharing the scatter’s gdp axis is a marginal: one column’s distribution, drawn along the edge of the plot that uses it. Put a second marginal on the right and the picture is the marginal plot, which most tools offer as a named chart type:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


(data(gapminder_2007) + bar * bin + x(gdp) + theme(height = 130)) /
  ((data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life)) |
     (data(gapminder_2007) + bar * bin + y(life) + theme(width = 130)))


((data(gapminder_2007) + bar * bin + x(col.gdp) + theme(height = 130)) /
  ((data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life)) |
     (data(gapminder_2007) + bar * bin + y(col.life) + theme(width = 130))))


(data(gapminder_2007) + bar * bin + x(:gdp) + theme(height = 130)) /
  ((data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life)) |
  (data(gapminder_2007) + bar * bin + y(:life) + theme(width = 130)))


below(plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(bar, bin), x(col.gdp),
  theme({ height: 130 })),
  beside(plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life)),
  plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(bar, bin), y(col.life),
  theme({ width: 130 }))))






                                      0 20 40 60  Count


                                                                                                                                                                            0K 20K 40K   40 50 60 70 80  Life Gdp


                                    0 10 20 30    Count






“Given gapminder 2007: bars derived by bin, x is gdp, above points, x is gdp, y is life, beside bars derived by bin, y is life.”
That figure is three ordinary plots and two operators. The top histogram shares gdp with the scatter, so its panel is drawn exactly as wide as the scatter’s. The right-hand one shares life, so its panel is exactly as tall as the scatter’s, and the life axis is drawn once, on the left. The empty top-right corner has no atom of its own. Both marginals stop where the scatter’s panel stops, and the corner is the room left over.
The marginals follow no special rule. bar * bin + y(life) is the histogram you already know. Its bars run left to right, because y now carries the bins and the count goes on x. The shared column need not be continuous either. Two plots reading the same category on x share its slots, so each category keeps the same place in both:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


(data(gapminder_2007) + box + x(continent) + y(life) + theme(height = 150)) /
  (data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(continent) + y(gdp) + color(continent))


((data(gapminder_2007) + box + x(col.continent) + y(col.life) + theme(height = 150)) /
  (data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.continent) + y(col.gdp) + color(col.continent)))


(data(gapminder_2007) + box + x(:continent) + y(:life) +
  theme(height = 150)) /
  (data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:continent) + y(:gdp) +
  color(:continent))


below(plot(data(gapminder_2007), box, x(col.continent), y(col.life),
  theme({ height: 150 })),
  plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.continent), y(col.gdp),
  color(col.continent)))






                                                                 40 50 60 70 80  Life


                                                                                                                                                                                  Asia Europe Africa Americas Oceania   0K 10K 20K 30K 40K 50K  Gdp Continent  Continent    Asia  Europe  Africa  Americas  Oceania 






“Given gapminder 2007: boxes, x is continent, y is life, above points, x is continent, y is gdp, color by continent.”
The five continents take the same slots in both panels, so each box is drawn directly above the countries it summarizes.

title: 29  Composition
section: 29.4 A clustered panel decides the order
text:
29.4 A clustered panel decides the order
A categorical axis needs an order, and most plots take the one the data arrived in. A panel with cluster computes a better one. cluster builds a tree of similar rows, and reading its leaves from left to right gives an order that puts similar things next to each other. When such a panel shares its axis, the shared axis takes that order.

A shared categorical axis takes the order a clustered panel computed for it.

The panels beside the clustered one stay plain, and their slots arrive in the tree’s order. gog refuses two panels that derive different orders for one shared axis, because one axis cannot hold two orders. Give both the same columns to cluster(), or cluster in one panel alone. The Cluster chapter uses this rule: a tile plot with a tree on two of its sides, each tree deciding one axis.

title: 29  Composition
section: 29.5 How thin is the marginal histogram? theme(width =, height =)
text:
29.5 How thin is the marginal histogram? theme(width =, height =)
A plot states how much room it wants in pixels, and the plots that ask for nothing split what is left. A page that states no size is 800 by 600 pixels, which is what a plot drawn alone takes. That is the whole of the sizing in the marginal plot: the top histogram asks for 130 pixels of height, and the scatter asks for nothing and takes the rest.
The same two arguments also size a plot drawn on its own, where the room being divided is the whole image:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) + theme(width = 420, height = 320)


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) + theme(width = 420, height = 320)


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life) +
  theme(width = 420, height = 320)


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life),
  theme({ width: 420, height: 320 }))






                                                                                                                                                                                  0K 10K 20K 30K 40K 50K   40 50 60 70 80  Life Gdp





That is Compositional Invariance, the sixth of the nine laws: one meaning in two places. A sentence that says a plot is 130 pixels tall says the same thing whether or not you compose it with another plot. Do not confuse theme(width =, height =) with theme(ratio = ). The second one shapes the panel inside the room the plot was given, and it never resizes the image.
Plots that ask for more height than the page has are refused, and the message gives both numbers:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) + theme(height = 500)) /
  (data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) + theme(height = 500))


((data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) + theme(height = 500)) /
  (data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) + theme(height = 500)))


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life) +
  theme(height = 500)) /
  (data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life) +
  theme(height = 500))


below(plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life),
  theme({ height: 500 })),
  plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life),
  theme({ height: 500 })))




Error:
! gog: the plots below each other ask for 1000px of height between them, and the page has 600. A `theme(height = )` on a composed plot is how much of the page that plot takes, so the ones that state it must leave room for the ones that do not.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.

title: 29  Composition
section: 29.6 How big is the page itself?
text:
29.6 How big is the page itself?
That refusal compared both plots with the page’s own height, so a page has a size of its own. Two plots set side by side divide the page’s width, and each one keeps the full height of the page. Each plot sits in a cell, and a cell in a side-by-side page is already as tall as the page. So a height written into one of those plots changes nothing. The height belongs to the page, so write it on the page:


RPythonJulia


((data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life)) |
   (data(gapminder_2007) + bar * count + x(continent))) + theme(height = 260)


(((data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life)) |
   (data(gapminder_2007) + bar * count + x(col.continent))) + theme(height = 260))


((data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life)) |
  (data(gapminder_2007) + bar * count + x(:continent))) +
  theme(height = 260)






                                                                                                                                                                                    0K 10K 20K 30K 40K 50K   40 50 60 70 80  Life Gdp


                              Asia Europe Africa Americas Oceania   0 20 40  Count Continent






Here the same two arguments are written on the page instead of on a plot. A page states how much room it wants, exactly as a plot does. When you compose them, the plot becomes one cell of the page.
This matters most where a mark cannot be stretched to fill its panel. A cube is drawn with one scale in both screen directions, so its shape is never stretched. A tall, narrow cell therefore draws the cube small, with empty bands above it and below it. The figure is then the wrong shape, and you correct it by sizing the page.
Size is the only thing a page can say. Every other property theme() sets describes a panel: its gridlines, its frame, its background, the angle its tick labels are read at. A page has no panel, so each of those properties is refused, and the refusal says to write it into the plot it describes:


RPythonJulia


((data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life)) |
  (data(gapminder_2007) + bar * count + x(continent))) + theme(grid = "none")


(((data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life)) |
  (data(gapminder_2007) + bar * count + x(col.continent))) + theme(grid = "none"))


((data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life)) |
  (data(gapminder_2007) + bar * count + x(:continent))) +
  theme(grid = "none")




Error:
! gog: `theme(grid = )` describes a panel, and a page is plots arranged rather than a panel of its own. On a page, `theme()` states how big the figure is — `theme(width = )` and `theme(height = )` — and nothing else. Write this into the plot it describes, before composing: `(plot + theme(grid = )) | other_plot`.

title: 29  Composition
text:
29.7 What a page is not
A title over two plots seems to belong to the page rather than to either plot, so you might try writing it there. A page is plots arranged, so anything belonging to one plot is written into that plot before it is composed. Apart from width and height, any atom added to a page is refused, and the message names where it belongs:


RPythonJulia


((data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life)) |
  (data(gapminder_2007) + bar * count + x(continent))) + title("Two views")


(((data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life)) |
  (data(gapminder_2007) + bar * count + x(col.continent))) + title("Two views"))


((data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life)) |
  (data(gapminder_2007) + bar * count + x(:continent))) +
  title("Two views")




Error:
! gog: `title()` belongs to a plot, and the left side is a page of them. Write it into the plot it describes, before composing: `(plot + title("...")) | other_plot`.


And a page cannot be faceted, because a facet splits one plot by a column and a page is not one plot:


RPythonJulia


((data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life)) |
  (data(gapminder_2007) + bar * count + x(continent))) | facet(continent)


(((data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life)) |
  (data(gapminder_2007) + bar * count + x(col.continent))) | facet(col.continent))


((data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life)) |
  (data(gapminder_2007) + bar * count + x(:continent))) |
  facet(:continent)




Error:
! gog: `|` faceted a page of plots, and a facet splits *one* plot by a column. Facet the plots before composing them: `(plot | facet(g)) | other_plot`.


Facet first, then compose: (plot | facet(g)) | other_plot is a faceted plot beside another plot, and it is legal.

title: 29  Composition
text:
29.8 Where these operators come from
Neither reading of | is this grammar’s invention, and the two were borrowed from different places.
The facet reading is the older of the two. Trellis display wrote a conditioned plot as y ~ x | g (Becker et al., 1996), and lattice writes it that way still. There the bar means “given”, the same meaning it has in conditional probability. That is exactly what plot | facet(continent) says.
The composition reading comes from patchwork (Pedersen, 2019). That package writes p1 | p2 for side by side and p1 / p2 for one above the other. gog spells composition the same way on purpose: a reader who already uses that package has little new to learn here, and a third spelling of a settled idea would only add work.
Composing pictures with operators is older than both of them. Henderson’s Functional Geometry (Henderson, 1982) describes an algebra of pictures, and its two combining operations are beside and above. Structure and Interpretation of Computer Programs (SICP) teaches the same picture language, and Haskell’s diagrams library spells the two operations ||| and ===. The JavaScript binding has no operators to overload, so it spells the two operations as words: beside(), and below() for what Henderson called above.
One divergence is worth naming, since Wilkinson settles most questions in this project. His graph algebra also has a /, and it means nest (a/b, “a within b”), not “below”. gog’s facet operators use his crossing and not his nesting, so / is free to mean the page here.

title: 29  Composition
text:
29.9 Layering, faceting, or composition?
The three answer different questions, so your data decides which one you want:

Layering when the marks are different tables on the same measurement. One coordinate space, one pair of axes, and the second table annotates the first: a threshold, a band, a label, a forecast. Data explains multi-table plots.
Faceting when the panels are the same measurement on different subsets. One scale, one legend, and you can compare the panels directly.
Composition when the plots are different measurements that belong on one page. Each keeps its own space, and the only thing they may share is a column.

Layering is the one you have to verify, because it is the only one the engine cannot check for you. A second table that measures something the axes do not measure still draws when you layer it. The columns resolve, the marks are drawn, and the picture is wrong. Sales figures on an income axis are a legal sentence. So if the second table does not measure what the axes measure, compose two plots instead of layering one onto the other.
A marginal plot is composition because the histogram and the scatter measure different things: one counts countries, the other puts each country at its own position. They share gdp, and that one shared column is what the shared-axis rule turns into a single axis.

title: 29  Composition
text:
29.10 In short
| and / mean faceting when a column splits one plot into panels, and composition when both sides are whole plots. A shared column becomes a shared axis, and plots that share nothing keep their own scales. A page arranges the plots it is given, and computes nothing of its own.

title: 29  Composition
text:
29.11 What comes next
Composition arranges finished plots, and each one still draws the rows it was given. Flow computes a picture instead. It carries one amount through a series of stages, and it reads those stages from the table’s own columns.




Becker, R. A., Cleveland, W. S., & Shyu, M.-J. (1996). The visual design and control of trellis display. Journal of Computational and Graphical Statistics, 5(2), 123–155. https://doi.org/10.1080/10618600.1996.10474701


Henderson, P. (1982). Functional geometry. In D. P. Friedman & D. S. Wise (Eds.), Conference record of the 1982 ACM symposium on lisp and functional programming (pp. 179–187). ACM Press.


Pedersen, T. L. (2019). patchwork: The composer of plots. R package; first CRAN release 1 December 2019. https://patchwork.data-imaginist.com/

title: 30  Flow
text:
30.1 One row is one path
Where did each part go? Some tables record movement: each row says that some amount started in one place and finished in another. A flow diagram draws that movement. The places are sorted into stages, drawn side by side, and bands carry each amount from stage to stage. The wider the band, the larger the amount it carries. The world calls this picture a Sankey diagram, or an alluvial diagram, and as with the pie there is no atom that spells either name.
A stage is one of the table’s categorical columns. Its distinct values are the possible places at that step, and each row sits in one of them. The flow transform computes the whole diagram from one table of such columns. This chapter builds the diagram one layer at a time, using the passengers and crew of the Titanic. titanic holds one row per group of people. The columns are class, sex, age (child or adult) and survived. The last column, n, is how many people the group held. The table has one row for every combination of those four columns, so some rows count zero people:
The first question of the Titanic table is who survived, and whether a passenger’s class changed how likely that was. That is a movement from a class to an outcome, which is a flow with two stages. Name the stages in the atom, left to right, and bind the count to y:
RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(titanic) + ribbon * flow(class, survived) + y(n) +
  title("Who survived, by class")


(data(titanic) + ribbon * flow(col["class"], col.survived) + y(col.n) +
  title("Who survived, by class"))


data(titanic) + ribbon * flow(:class, :survived) + y(:n) +
  title("Who survived, by class")


plot(data(titanic), layer(ribbon, flow(col.class, col.survived)),
  y(col.n), title("Who survived, by class"))






                                class survived   500 1000 1500  Who survived, by class N
“Given titanic: ribbons derived by flow through class and survived, y is n.”
Each band is one path through the stages. No slot carries a name yet, so find a path by its position. The slots stack from the bottom in each column’s order, so the lowest band leaves the 1st slot and arrives at the Yes slot. It carries the 203 first-class passengers who survived, and it holds that thickness at both ends. Rows that share a path are added together. The four 1st rows that end in Yes differ only in sex and age, and the atom names neither, so the four become one band.
The stages are drawn along the horizontal axis, each named by its column. x() has nothing left to set: the atom’s argument order is the order the stages are drawn in. The vertical axis is the count, with the same ticks any other plot would get. The bands at each stage stack from zero with no gaps, so the top edge of any band gives the total of that band and every band under it.

title: 30  Flow
text:
30.2 Adding a stage
The next question is whether women survived more often than men. The two-stage diagram cannot answer it, because nothing in it records a person’s sex. Add a stage by adding a column. Each path now crosses three stages, and each band still carries one path’s count at both of its ends:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(titanic) + ribbon * flow(class, sex, survived) + y(n) +
  title("Class, then sex, then survival")


(data(titanic) + ribbon * flow(col["class"], col.sex, col.survived) + y(col.n) +
  title("Class, then sex, then survival"))


data(titanic) + ribbon * flow(:class, :sex, :survived) + y(:n) +
  title("Class, then sex, then survival")


plot(data(titanic), layer(ribbon, flow(col.class, col.sex, col.survived)),
  y(col.n), title("Class, then sex, then survival"))






                                                          class sex survived   0K 1K 2K  Class, then sex, then survival N





“Given titanic: ribbons derived by flow through class, sex and survived, y is n.”
Each band is now one group of people, and it reports three things about them: their class, whether they were male or female, and whether they survived. The band from 1st through Female to Yes carries 141 people. That is how many women in first class survived.

title: 30  Flow
text:
30.3 Color comes from a stage
With three stages the bands cross one another, and a path is hard to follow through a crossing unless something marks it. A band runs through every stage, so any stage can color it. Write color() after the ribbon layer and name the stage whose value gives each band its color:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(titanic) + ribbon * flow(class, sex, survived) + y(n) + color(class) +
  title("The same paths, colored by class")


(data(titanic) + ribbon * flow(col["class"], col.sex, col.survived) + y(col.n) + color(col["class"]) +
  title("The same paths, colored by class"))


data(titanic) + ribbon * flow(:class, :sex, :survived) + y(:n) +
  color(:class) + title("The same paths, colored by class")


plot(data(titanic), layer(ribbon, flow(col.class, col.sex, col.survived)),
  y(col.n), color(col.class), title("The same paths, colored by class"))






                                                          class sex survived   0K 1K 2K  The same paths, colored by class N  Class    1st  2nd  3rd  Crew 





“Given titanic: ribbons derived by flow through class, sex and survived, y is n, color by class.”
Coloring by class gives each band the color of the slot it starts from. You can then see which classes meet in each later slot. Coloring by survived would instead color every band by how its path ends. Only a stage can color a band, because a band is a whole path, and only a stage holds a value every path carries.

title: 30  Flow
text:
30.4 The slots and their names
So far you have found a path by its position, because no slot carries a name. Two more layers finish the diagram. A zone layer draws each stage’s slots, the stacked blocks the bands leave and arrive at. A text layer names them. The three layers name the same computation, so they always agree about where everything sits:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(titanic) + y(n) +
  ribbon * flow(class, sex, survived) + color(class) +
  zone * flow(class, sex, survived) + style(color = "gray") +
  text * flow(class, sex, survived) + label(name) +
  title("The full diagram: bands, slots, names")


(data(titanic) + y(col.n) +
  ribbon * flow(col["class"], col.sex, col.survived) + color(col["class"]) +
  zone * flow(col["class"], col.sex, col.survived) + style(color = "gray") +
  text * flow(col["class"], col.sex, col.survived) + label(col.name) +
  title("The full diagram: bands, slots, names"))


data(titanic) + y(:n) + ribbon * flow(:class, :sex, :survived) +
  color(:class) + zone * flow(:class, :sex, :survived) +
  style(color = "gray") + text * flow(:class, :sex, :survived) +
  label(:name) + title("The full diagram: bands, slots, names")


plot(data(titanic), y(col.n),
  layer(ribbon, flow(col.class, col.sex, col.survived)), color(col.class),
  layer(zone, flow(col.class, col.sex, col.survived)),
  style({ color: "gray" }),
  layer(text, flow(col.class, col.sex, col.survived)), label(col.name),
  title("The full diagram: bands, slots, names"))






                                                        1st 2nd 3rd Crew Male Female Yes No               class sex survived   0K 1K 2K  The full diagram: bands, slots, names N  Class    1st  2nd  3rd  Crew 





“Given titanic: y is n, ribbons derived by flow through class, sex and survived, color by class, and also zones derived by flow through class, sex and survived, and text derived by flow through class, sex and survived, label by name.”
The slots take their color from style(), gray here so that only the bands carry color. The names come from label(name): the transform writes each slot’s name into a column called name, exactly as partition does.
The count on y is optional. Bind nothing and every row counts as 1, so the diagram counts rows instead of summing a column. partition uses that default too, and count tallies rows the same way. This table needs y(n). It holds one row per combination, so counting its rows would count combinations rather than people.

title: 30  Flow
text:
30.5 What flow refuses
A flow needs at least two stages, because movement needs a place to start and a place to finish:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(titanic) + y(n) + ribbon * flow(class)


data(titanic) + y(col.n) + ribbon * flow(col["class"])


data(titanic) + y(:n) + ribbon * flow(:class)


plot(data(titanic), y(col.n), layer(ribbon, flow(col.class)))




Error:
! gog: `flow()` needs at least two stage columns, in reading order — `flow(class, sex, survived)` runs each row from its `class` to its `survived`. One column has no between.


The stage axis is drawn from the atom’s own columns, so a bound x has nothing left to set:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(titanic) + x(n) + ribbon * flow(class, survived)


data(titanic) + x(col.n) + ribbon * flow(col["class"], col.survived)


data(titanic) + x(:n) + ribbon * flow(:class, :survived)


plot(data(titanic), x(col.n),
  layer(ribbon, flow(col.class, col.survived)))




Error:
! gog: under `flow` the stage axis is drawn from the atom's own columns, so `x(...)` has nothing left to say. Remove it — to reorder the stages, reorder `flow(...)`'s arguments.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


Only three marks can read what flow computes, and the refusal lists all three when another mark is used:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(titanic) + y(n) + bar * flow(class, survived)


data(titanic) + y(col.n) + bar * flow(col["class"], col.survived)


data(titanic) + y(:n) + bar * flow(:class, :survived)


plot(data(titanic), y(col.n), layer(bar, flow(col.class, col.survived)))




Error:
! gog: `flow` lays a path's magnitude through its stages — an interval at each stage, and a band between adjacent ones — and `bar` has no reading for that. Three marks do: `ribbon * flow(<a>, <b>)` draws the bands, `zone * flow(<a>, <b>)` draws each stage's slots, and `text * flow(<a>, <b>) + label(name)` names them. Bind `y(<amount>)` to weigh the paths, or bind nothing and each row counts 1.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


And the column that colors a band must be one of the stages. A column outside the stages holds no value a whole path shares:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(titanic) + y(n) + ribbon * flow(class, survived) + color(n)


data(titanic) + y(col.n) + ribbon * flow(col["class"], col.survived) + color(col.n)


data(titanic) + y(:n) + ribbon * flow(:class, :survived) + color(:n)


plot(data(titanic), y(col.n),
  layer(ribbon, flow(col.class, col.survived)), color(col.n))




Error:
! gog: `color(n)` under `flow` must name one of the atom's stages — a band is a path through them, and only a stage holds a value every band carries. Name one of `class`, `survived`, or set the paint for the whole layer with `style()`.
gog: `color(n)` maps a continuous (numeric) column, but `color` on `ribbon` needs a categorical (text) column.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.

title: 30  Flow
text:
30.6 Where the limits are
Every mark that draws on the page also bends into a circle, so asking for a bent flow is a reasonable thing to do. That bend is polar(), and a flow inside it is valid grammar. The bands bent around a circle are the chord diagram, which this engine does not draw:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(titanic) + y(n) + ribbon * flow(class, survived) + polar()


data(titanic) + y(col.n) + ribbon * flow(col["class"], col.survived) + polar()


data(titanic) + y(:n) + ribbon * flow(:class, :survived) + polar()


plot(data(titanic), y(col.n),
  layer(ribbon, flow(col.class, col.survived)), polar())




Error:
! gog: `flow` in `polar()` is valid grammar — the bands bent round a rim are the chord diagram — but this engine does not draw it yet. Draw the flow flat, or wait for the feature.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


The input has a limit too. A flow reads its stages as columns of one table, and each row names the place it holds at every stage. Some tools accept a different shape: a list of nodes, which are these slots, and a list of links between them. That shape can also describe flows that merge, skip a stage, or return to a stage they already visited. gog does not read it. The stage-column shape decides three things by itself. Every path passes through every stage, the totals match at each one, and no path can return to a stage it already visited.

title: 30  Flow
text:
30.7 What comes next
A flow needs its stages named, in the order you want them read. Cluster works the order out instead, joining the closest categories first and putting an axis in the tree’s order.

title: 31  Cluster
text:
31.1 The tree
Which categories in a table are most alike? A table of numbers holds the answer, but a reader cannot see it in the rows. The cluster transform computes it. It treats each category of an axis as a leaf of a tree. It finds the two closest leaves and joins them into one branch. Then it looks again, treating that new branch as a single thing, and joins the closest two again. It repeats until one tree holds every leaf. The world calls the picture a dendrogram, and as with the pie there is no atom that spells the name.
This chapter builds the tree, then uses it to order a tile plot. nutrients holds one row per pair of food and nutrient. There are eight everyday foods, and each one is measured on five nutrients:
Which two of the eight foods are most alike, and which one is least like all the rest? To answer that, the engine needs to know what to compare. Each leaf is described by a profile. cluster(amount, over = nutrient) says that one leaf’s profile is its amount in every category of nutrient. So each food’s profile is five numbers, and those five numbers give the position of one point. The distance between two leaves is the straight-line distance between their two points. Two branches join at an average distance. Measure from every leaf on one branch to every leaf on the other, and average all of those distances.
RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(nutrients) + path * cluster(amount, over = nutrient) + x(food) +
  title("Eight foods, joined by what they are made of")


(data(nutrients) + path * cluster(col.amount, over=col.nutrient) + x(col.food) +
  title("Eight foods, joined by what they are made of"))


data(nutrients) + path * cluster(:amount, over = :nutrient) + x(:food) +
  title("Eight foods, joined by what they are made of")


plot(data(nutrients),
  layer(path, cluster(col.amount, { over: col.nutrient })), x(col.food),
  title("Eight foods, joined by what they are made of"))






                                           chicken salmon spinach oats rice beans lentils almonds   0 20 40  Eight foods, joined by what they are made of Distance Food
“Given nutrients: paths derived by cluster on amount, over nutrient, x is food.”
path draws the tree. A tree is a set of points that only make the right shape when they are joined in a fixed order. path is the mark that keeps that order, because it strokes the rows as the table gives them. Here x(food) is the bound position, so x carries the leaves, and this chapter calls it the leaf axis. You bind nothing to the other position, and cluster supplies it. The transform computes the distance at which each pair of branches joins, and it names that axis Distance. The place where two branches meet is a join. The further a join is drawn from the leaf axis, the more different the two branches are. Beans and lentils join lowest, and rice and oats join just above them. Almonds join highest of all, which makes almonds the food least like the rest.
Bind y instead of x, and the same tree is drawn sideways, with the leaves down the left edge:
RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(nutrients) + path * cluster(amount, over = nutrient) + y(food)


data(nutrients) + path * cluster(col.amount, over=col.nutrient) + y(col.food)


data(nutrients) + path * cluster(:amount, over = :nutrient) + y(:food)


plot(data(nutrients),
  layer(path, cluster(col.amount, { over: col.nutrient })), y(col.food))






                                           0 20 40   almonds lentils beans rice oats spinach salmon chicken  Food Distance
“Given nutrients: paths derived by cluster on amount, over nutrient, y is food.”
Three things about how cluster builds the tree cannot be changed. Distance is measured on the values as they are, with no rescaling first. Fat runs from 0.3 to 49.9 and iron from 0.5 to 3.7, so fat has far more effect on the distance than iron does. If you want every nutrient to count equally, rescale the columns where your data lives. Branches join at their average distance, so every join is further from the leaf axis than the joins it holds. And two leaves with identical profiles join at zero, so their join is drawn on the leaf axis itself.

title: 31  Cluster
text:
31.2 The order
Reading the finished tree along the leaf axis also gives an order, with similar foods next to each other. That order is worth having on a tile plot, because a pattern in the tiles is hard to see when similar foods are far apart. A tile plot of the same table draws its slots in the order the rows arrived. Nothing chose that order:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(nutrients) + zone + x(food) + y(nutrient) + color(amount) +
  title("In the order the rows arrived")


(data(nutrients) + zone + x(col.food) + y(col.nutrient) + color(col.amount) +
  title("In the order the rows arrived"))


data(nutrients) + zone + x(:food) + y(:nutrient) + color(:amount) +
  title("In the order the rows arrived")


plot(data(nutrients), zone, x(col.food), y(col.nutrient),
  color(col.amount), title("In the order the rows arrived"))






                                                                                salmon rice almonds lentils chicken spinach beans oats   iron fiber carbs fat protein  In the order the rows arrived Nutrient Food  Amount         49.90 24.95 0 





“Given nutrients: zones, x is food, y is nutrient, color by amount.”
zone * cluster draws the same tiles. The leaf axis now runs in the tree’s order. Chicken and salmon are next to each other on the left, and the four foods that are mostly carbohydrate are together between spinach and almonds:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(nutrients) + zone * cluster(over = nutrient) +
  x(food) + y(nutrient) + color(amount) +
  title("In the tree's order")


(data(nutrients) + zone * cluster(over=col.nutrient) +
  x(col.food) + y(col.nutrient) + color(col.amount) +
  title("In the tree's order"))


data(nutrients) + zone * cluster(over = :nutrient) + x(:food) +
  y(:nutrient) + color(:amount) + title("In the tree's order")


plot(data(nutrients), layer(zone, cluster({ over: col.nutrient })),
  x(col.food), y(col.nutrient), color(col.amount),
  title("In the tree's order"))






                                                                                chicken salmon spinach oats rice beans lentils almonds   iron fiber carbs fat protein  In the tree's order Nutrient Food  Amount         49.90 24.95 0 





“Given nutrients: zones derived by cluster over nutrient, x is food, y is nutrient, color by amount.”
On a tile plot the values are already bound to color, so cluster need not name them again. over names the profile column. The other categorical axis holds the leaves, and that is the axis the tree reorders.

title: 31  Cluster
text:
31.3 The clustered heatmap
So far one tree has ordered one axis. Put a tree on both sides of the tiles, and both axes take an order, so you can see where each one came from. The world calls the result a clustered heatmap. It is three plots joined by two operators: a tree above, the tile plot below it, and a second tree to the right of the legend. The alignment comes from one rule in Composition: a shared categorical axis takes the order a clustered panel computed for it. The tile plot in the middle carries no cluster of its own. It is the same plain tile plot drawn earlier in this chapter. Its column order arrives from the tree above, and its row order from the tree on the right.


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


(data(nutrients) + path * cluster(amount, over = nutrient) + x(food) +
   theme(height = 150)) /
  ((data(nutrients) + zone + x(food) + y(nutrient) + color(amount)) |
     (data(nutrients) + path * cluster(amount, over = food) + y(nutrient) +
        theme(width = 150)))


((data(nutrients) + path * cluster(col.amount, over=col.nutrient) + x(col.food) +
   theme(height = 150)) /
  ((data(nutrients) + zone + x(col.food) + y(col.nutrient) + color(col.amount)) |
     (data(nutrients) + path * cluster(col.amount, over=col.food) + y(col.nutrient) +
        theme(width = 150))))


(data(nutrients) + path * cluster(:amount, over = :nutrient) + x(:food) +
  theme(height = 150)) /
  ((data(nutrients) + zone + x(:food) + y(:nutrient) + color(:amount)) |
  (data(nutrients) + path * cluster(:amount, over = :food) +
  y(:nutrient) + theme(width = 150)))


below(plot(data(nutrients),
  layer(path, cluster(col.amount, { over: col.nutrient })), x(col.food),
  theme({ height: 150 })),
  beside(plot(data(nutrients), zone, x(col.food), y(col.nutrient),
  color(col.amount)),
  plot(data(nutrients),
  layer(path, cluster(col.amount, { over: col.food })), y(col.nutrient),
  theme({ width: 150 }))))






                                       0 20 40  Distance


                                                                                chicken salmon spinach oats rice beans lentils almonds   carbs fiber iron protein fat  Nutrient Food  Amount         49.90 24.95 0 


                                 0 10 20 30 40    Distance






“Given nutrients: paths derived by cluster on amount, over nutrient, x is food, above zones, x is food, y is nutrient, color by amount, beside paths derived by cluster on amount, over food, y is nutrient.”
Each column of tiles is one food. Read the tree directly above a column, and it shows which foods that one joined first. The trees are not decoration. They decide which foods end up next to each other.

title: 31  Cluster
text:
31.4 What cluster refuses
You met order() on a bar chart, where it sorted the categories along an axis. You may want to write it here as well. An axis holds one order. order() sorts by a column, cluster derives an order from the tree, and writing both is a contradiction:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(nutrients) + path * cluster(amount, over = nutrient) + x(food) +
  order(food)


(data(nutrients) + path * cluster(col.amount, over=col.nutrient) + x(col.food) +
  order(col.food))


data(nutrients) + path * cluster(:amount, over = :nutrient) + x(:food) +
  order(:food)


plot(data(nutrients),
  layer(path, cluster(col.amount, { over: col.nutrient })), x(col.food),
  order(col.food))




Error:
! gog: `order(food)` and `cluster` both order the `food` axis — one sorts by a column, the other derives the order from the tree, and an axis holds one order. Drop one.

title: 31  Cluster
text:
31.6 What comes next
A cluster reorders an axis, and the plot still uses two positions. Space adds the third position, z, which lifts the marks off the page into a cube you can turn.

title: 32  Space
text:
32.1 z: one more vowel
What do you do when a third measurement matters as much as the first two? Every plot so far has been drawn on a plane: a mark, an x, a y. The grammar has a third position channel, z. Binding it is enough to lift the mark off the page.
Here are three flower measurements. Two of them make an ordinary scatter, and the species already begin to separate, but versicolor and virginica still blur together along the diagonal:

  color(col.species))

“Given the iris flowers: points, x is petal length, y is sepal length, color by species.”
Now add the third measurement as z. Nothing else about the sentence changes (the same point, the same x and y, one more vowel), and the plot lifts into space:
RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(iris_flowers) + point +
  x(petal_length) + y(sepal_length) + z(sepal_width) + color(species)

  x(col.petal_length) + y(col.sepal_length) + z(col.sepal_width) + color(col.species))

  z(:sepal_width) + color(:species)
