                                                                                                                                                                          1K 10K   40 50 60 70 80  Life Gdp  Continent    Asia  Europe  Africa  Americas  Oceania
“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp on a log scale, y is life, color by continent.”
That is the sentence from A first plot, with a colon in front of each column. In this grammar a plain string spells a value, as in style(color = "tomato") or palette("okabe"). A symbol is visibly not a string, so the colon does the same work as R’s bare name and Python’s col. accessor. The grammar’s oldest rule is that a channel takes a column and never a value. In Julia the syntax itself enforces it, so no check has to.
So a string where a column belongs is refused, and told what to write:
data(gapminder_2007) + point + x("gdp") + y(:life)
gog: `x("gdp")` binds a *value*, and a channel takes a *column*. In Julia a column is a symbol, which is what keeps the two apart: `x(:gdp)` maps the column called `gdp`.
The mistake in the other direction is refused the same way, and for the same reason (Setting vs mapping):
data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life) + style(color = :continent)
gog: `style(color = )` fixes one value for the whole layer, and `:continent` is a column. To *map* it — one value per category, with a legend to decode it — that is a channel: `color(:continent)`.
A column name Julia cannot read as an identifier, because it holds a space or a dot, is written Symbol("life exp"). A name in another writing system needs no such thing: :지역 (jiyeok, region) is an ordinary symbol, because Julia identifiers are Unicode.

title: 48  Julia
text:
48.2 A sentence over several lines
A long sentence can be broken across lines, and Julia asks for nothing extra. Like R, it continues a line that ends in +:


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp, scale = "log") + y(:life) +
    color(:continent) +
    size(:population)


                                                                                                                                                                          1K 10K   40 50 60 70 80  Life Gdp  Continent    Asia  Europe  Africa  Americas  Oceania   Population    199.6K  659.4M  1.3B 




“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp on a log scale, y is life, color by continent, size by population.”
What does not work is the opposite arrangement, where a line starts with the operator. Julia ends the statement at the line break and reads the next line on its own, so it reports an error about + instead of drawing. To write a sentence that way, wrap the whole of it in parentheses. That is what Python requires for every multi-line sentence (Python), and inside parentheses a line may begin with + in Julia too.

title: 48  Julia
text:
48.3 The operators, and their precedence
Julia’s precedence table is not R’s. R puts | below +; Julia puts it in the addition tier, alongside +. That could have broken every faceted sentence in this book, so it was measured rather than assumed:



Written
Julia builds
R builds




a + b + c \| d
(a + b + c) \| d
the same


a \| b / c
a \| (b / c)
the same


a * b + c
(a * b) + c
the same


a \| b + c
(a \| b) + c
a \| (b + c)



Only the last row differs, and it is the row where an atom is written after a |. A facet sentence never does that, and R refuses it anyway. A composed page comes closer, because the plot on the right names its own table and then adds atoms to it. So every composed page in this book is written in parentheses, and they close the right-hand plot before the | is read. The first row is safe for a different reason: Julia reads operators of one tier from left to right, so everything left of the | is joined first.
Faceting therefore reads exactly as it does in R:


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp, scale = "log") + y(:life) | facet(:continent)


                                                             1K 10K   40 50 60 70 80                                                      1K 10K                                                                              1K 10K                                                   1K 10K                            1K 10K      Asia  Europe  Africa  Americas  Oceania  Life Gdp




“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp on a log scale, y is life, split into panel columns by continent.”
A transform reads the same way, because * binds tighter than +:


data(gapminder_2007) + bar * mean + x(:continent) + y(:life)


                                  Asia Europe Africa Americas Oceania   0 20 40 60 80  Life Continent




“Given gapminder 2007: bars derived by mean, x is continent, y is life.”

title: 48  Julia
text:
48.4 Nine names Julia already uses
Nine of the kernel’s words are also names in Base: count, sum, min, max, range, size, step, stack and map. Julia will not choose between two modules that export the same name, and the rule is the language’s own. Writing one of these nine without an import gives an UndefVarError with a hint, rather than the wrong function. That is the safe outcome, and it means one more import line:
using GrammarOfGraphics
using GrammarOfGraphics: count, sum, min, max, range, size, step, stack, map
Those two lines open every block on this page that drew a plot. With them in place, a gog sentence builds and Base.sum still answers:


println(bar * bin)
println(Base.sum([1, 2, 3]))
<gog bar>
6


bin is not in the import line, because Base.bin is not exported, so there is no second bin to choose between.
The import line treats the nine names alike, but their effect on code you already wrote is not equal, and map is where that shows. Base.map appears in ordinary Julia code constantly, while Base.step and Base.stack appear far less often. Code you already wrote that calls map now reaches gog’s map instead, and the error names a line you did not change. Write Base.map there, and the same prefix works for any of the nine.
Every language meets this problem, and each one asks you to solve it differently. R’s range, sum and min belong to base R, Python’s bin, sum and max are builtins, and Julia’s belong to Base. A grammar keeps its own vocabulary; what changes is how each language asks you to say which one you meant.

title: 48  Julia
text:
48.5 The table
A table is a named tuple of columns, so a first plot needs nothing installed:


data((person = ["Ada", "Alan", "Grace"], cm = [160.0, 172.0, 181.0]),
     name = "heights") + bar + x(:person) + y(:cm)


                            Ada Alan Grace   0 50 100 150  Cm Person




A Dict works too, and so does anything that implements names and [!, col], which is what a DataFrame does. The package never imports DataFrames, so a reader who does not use one installs nothing extra. gog_table("gapminder_2007") fetches any of the book’s shared tables, as it does in the other three languages (The book’s data).
Julia has both a Date and a DateTime, as R and Python do. A Date column gets day ticks, and a DateTime column keeps its hours and minutes. The engine reads the unit off the type, so nothing is guessed.
R reads a table’s name off the expression you wrote, and Julia cannot. An unnamed table gets a generated name instead, such as data2. A warning or a refusal names the table it is about, so write data(df, name = "notes") when you want that message to say notes (Data).

title: 48  Julia
text:
48.6 Reading from a database
query() takes a DBInterface.jl connection. That is Julia’s database standard, and it covers SQLite.jl, LibPQ.jl, MySQL.jl and DuckDB.jl.
using DBInterface, SQLite, GrammarOfGraphics

con = SQLite.DB("sales.db")
query(con, "SELECT status, revenue FROM orders") + bar + x(:status) + y(:revenue)
One detail is specific to this binding. GrammarOfGraphics does not depend on DBInterface. Every dependency the package declares is a Julia standard library, and a database package would be the first exception. Every reader would install it, and many never write SQL. So the package finds DBInterface in your session instead.
In practice this means one extra line: you must write using DBInterface yourself. Without it, query() names the missing package and the line that fixes it, rather than failing later with a message about something else.

title: 48  Julia
text:
48.7 Getting it
The Julia package is named GrammarOfGraphics. The name is longer than the one R and Python use, and the registry is the reason. Julia’s registry checks a new name automatically, and that check asks for at least five letters in capitalized words. A lowercase gog fails on both counts.
Installing takes one command. A plot is drawn by the engine, which is a compiled Rust binary, and every one of the four packages carries one. Python and JavaScript ship it, and R builds or bundles it. Julia fetches it as an artifact, which is how a Julia package distributes a binary. Pkg downloads the build for your computer along with the package, so there is nothing else to install.
using Pkg
Pkg.add("GrammarOfGraphics")
To work from a checkout instead, add the package from the path where it sits:
using Pkg
Pkg.develop(path = "jl-pkg/GrammarOfGraphics")

using GrammarOfGraphics
The engine is looked for in five places, in this order: the GOG_CLI_PATH environment variable, the artifact the install fetched, a copy you placed inside the package yourself, gog-cli on your PATH, and a local target/release build. The search stops at the first place that holds the engine. An installed copy finds the artifact and never looks further. A checkout has no artifact, so the search runs to the end of the list and uses the build you compiled yourself.
render_svg(plot) returns the SVG as a string, and a plot displays itself in a notebook, because the binding hands the notebook a picture when it asks for one.

title: 48  Julia
text:
48.8 What comes next
The first three languages write one sentence three ways, differing only in how a column is named. JavaScript is the one that reads differently, because it cannot overload + * | / and spells them as four words.

title: 49  JavaScript
text:
49.1 The comma is +
The grammar does not change when the language does. One engine reads one specification, so a sentence means the same thing no matter who wrote it. Everything in this book up to here is as true in JavaScript as it is in R.
The sentence is spelled differently here, and the operators are the reason. Every other binding joins the same words with the same four operators. JavaScript cannot join words that way, because +, *, | and / cannot be given a meaning on objects. a + b joins two objects into one piece of text, a * b is NaN, and a | b is a bitwise integer. There is no version of the language in which data(gm) + point builds a plot.
So JavaScript spells the four operators as four words. That is the change this chapter starts from. Read the two lines side by side first:
Every JavaScript block with a plot under it was executed, through the same engine every other chapter uses.
A gog sentence is a list of words, and in JavaScript it is a list of arguments. The commas mean nothing on their own. Inside plot() they join the words, exactly as + joins them in R. A named argument is written differently: it goes into an object at the end of the call, which A named argument is one trailing object sets out in full.

plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp, { scale: 'log' }), y(col.life), color(col.continent))


                                                                                                                                                                          1K 10K   40 50 60 70 80  Life Gdp  Continent    Asia  Europe  Africa  Americas  Oceania
“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp on a log scale, y is life, color by continent.”
Those are the words of A first plot, in the same order, reading the same way. Position still decides scope (Encoding scope), so a channel written after a mark belongs to that mark and one written before belongs to the plot. The commas change nothing about that; they are the + signs.

title: 49  JavaScript
text:
49.2 layer() is *
In R, * binds tighter than +, which is how bar * bin + x(life) reads as a binned bar rather than a bar plus a bin. JavaScript has no precedence to use here, so the tighter binding becomes nesting:


plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(bar, mean), x(col.continent), y(col.life))


                                  Asia Europe Africa Americas Oceania   0 20 40 60 80  Life Continent




“Given gapminder 2007: bars derived by mean, x is continent, y is life.”
Nesting is the clearer of the two. A reader who does not already know that * binds tighter than + has to be told; a reader looking at layer(bar, mean) can see it.
Just over half the sentences in this book need no layer() at all, because they are a flat list of words. Where one is needed, it almost always holds two words:


plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(bar, count), x(col.continent), style({ color: 'steelblue' }))


                              Asia Europe Africa Americas Oceania   0 20 40  Count Continent




“Given gapminder 2007: bars derived by count, x is continent.”

title: 49  JavaScript
text:
49.3 across() and down() are | and /
Faceting in R is plot | facet(era), panels side by side, or plot / facet(era), panels stacked. In R, facet() means nothing on its own: it always follows a | or a /. JavaScript writes that whole phrase as one word:


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp, { scale: 'log' }), y(col.life), across(col.continent))


                                                             1K 10K   40 50 60 70 80                                                      1K 10K                                                                              1K 10K                                                   1K 10K                            1K 10K      Asia  Europe  Africa  Americas  Oceania  Life Gdp




“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp on a log scale, y is life, split into panel columns by continent.”
down() stacks the panels instead. Writing both gives a grid: one panel column per value of the first column, and one panel row per value of the second. That is what plot | facet(a) / facet(b) does in R.
Because the pair is one word here, there is no separate facet() to write. Writing facet() from memory is refused, and the message names the word to use instead:


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life), facet(col.continent))
gog: JavaScript has no `facet()`, because it has no `|` or `/` to join it with — the pair is one word here. Panels side by side: `across(col.continent)`. Panels stacked: `down(col.continent)`.

title: 49  JavaScript
section: 49.4 Composing two plots: beside() and below()
text:
49.4 Composing two plots: beside() and below()
The | you have just replaced had a second job in R. What is on its right decides which job it does: plot | facet(g) splits one plot into panels, and plot_a | plot_b arranges two plots on a page. JavaScript has no | to overload, so nothing has to decide between those two meanings. The second one gets its own word, beside(), and below() for /:


below(plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(bar, bin), x(col.gdp), theme({ height: 130 })), plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life)))


                                      0 20 40 60  Count


                                                                                                                                                                            0K 20K 40K   40 50 60 70 80  Life Gdp





“Given gapminder 2007: bars derived by bin, x is gdp, above points, x is gdp, y is life.”
The two words come from an older algebra. Henderson’s Functional Geometry (Henderson, 1982) combines pictures with beside and above, and below() is this book’s name for above. Composition tells that story in full. Both words take pages as well as plots, so below(top, beside(main, right)) is the marginal plot, exactly as top / (main | right) is in R. The spelling does not decide what two composed plots share; the engine does. The same column on the aligned axis of both is one axis.

title: 49  JavaScript
text:
49.5 A column is written col.gdp
The operators are the whole of what JavaScript changes about a sentence. Two smaller differences are left, and the first is how a column is named. R writes a column as a bare name, Julia as a symbol, Python and JavaScript through a small accessor. The two languages with no bare names give the same answer, and for the same reason. In this grammar a plain string is how you spell a value, as in style({ color: "tomato" }), title("…"), palette("okabe"). Without the accessor a column and a value would look identical. The grammar’s oldest rule, that a channel takes a column and never a value, would then be invisible in the two languages that most need it stated.
So a string where a column belongs is refused, and the message says what to write:


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x('gdp'), y(col.life))
gog: `x("gdp")` binds a *value*, and a channel takes a *column*. JavaScript has no bare names, so a column is written with the accessor: `x(col.gdp)` maps the column called `gdp`.


The message names the spelling to write, because a string here is a value and a channel takes a column (Setting vs mapping). The mistake in the other direction is refused the same way:


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life), style({ color: col.continent }))
gog: `style({ color: … })` fixes one value for the whole layer, and `col.continent` is a column. To *map* it — one value per category, with a legend to decode it — that is a channel: `color(col.continent)`.


A column name with a space or a dot in it is not a JavaScript identifier. Write it in the bracket form instead: col["life exp"]. A name in another writing system needs no such thing: col.지역 (jiyeok, region) is an ordinary identifier.

title: 49  JavaScript
section: 49.6 A named argument is one trailing object
text:
49.6 A named argument is one trailing object
R writes x(gdp, scale = "log"). JavaScript has no syntax for a named argument. The named ones gather into a single object at the end, and the positional ones stay where they are:


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp, { scale: 'log', base: 2 }), y(col.life), title('Doublings of income'))


                                                                                                                                                                                      256 512 1024 2048 4096 8192 16384 32768   40 50 60 70 80  Doublings of income Life Gdp




“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp on a log scale in base 2, y is life.”
style() is the case where every argument is named, so it is written as one object throughout the book: style({ color: "tomato", size: 3 }).

title: 49  JavaScript
text:
49.7 The table, and its name
A table is an object of columns, { person: ['Ada', 'Alan', 'Grace'], cm: [160, 172, 181] }, so a first plot needs nothing installed:


plot(data(heights), bar, x(col.person), y(col.cm))


                            Ada Alan Grace   0 50 100 150  Cm Person




R reads the table’s name from the expression you wrote, and Python from the variable you passed. JavaScript can do neither, and the name matters: a layer resolves its columns against the nearest table by that name (Data). So an unnamed table is given a name of its own, which is enough to tell two tables in one sentence apart. Write data(df, { name: "notes" }) when a message should say notes rather than data2.

title: 49  JavaScript
49  JavaScript
49  JavaScript
text:
49.10 Getting it
A plot is drawn by the engine, which is a compiled Rust binary, so the npm package has to be able to find one.
npm install grammar-of-graphics
That command works today. The package is on npm, and the name is spelled out because npm already had a package called gog. The registry also forbids capital letters in a new name, so this is Julia’s GrammarOfGraphics written the way npm writes names.
The engine arrives with it. There are five more packages on npm, one per platform, each holding the engine compiled for that platform, and the main package lists all five as optional dependencies. The install takes the one that matches your computer and skips the other four. So there is nothing to put on your PATH, nothing to build, and no Rust toolchain to install.
The binding itself only builds the specification and hands it to that engine, and it depends on nothing else:
import { plot, data, point, x, y, col, render_svg } from "grammar-of-graphics";

const gm = { gdp: [1000, 2000, 3000], life: [60, 70, 80] };
console.log(render_svg(plot(data(gm), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life))));
render_svg() returns the SVG as a string. In a browser that string goes straight into the DOM, and on a server it is sent as the response. Nothing has to open a viewer window, and nothing has to be turned into pixels first. What the engine returns is already the finished thing.
To work from a checkout instead, build the engine once and import the package from where it sits:
cargo build --release -p gog-cli
import { plot, data, point, x, y, col, render_svg } from "./js-pkg/gog/src/index.js";
The engine is looked for in four places, in this order: the GOG_CLI_PATH environment variable, the platform package installed beside this one, gog-cli on your PATH, and a target/release build in a surrounding checkout. The second and third are how an installed copy works; GOG_CLI_PATH is how this page was rendered.

title: 49  JavaScript
section: 49.11 A plot for a web page: html_block()

title: 49  JavaScript
text:
49.12 What comes next
These four chapters are about spelling, and none of them changes what a sentence means. The afterword closes the book with the ten-day challenge, and the one goal the project has not built yet.




Henderson, P. (1982). Functional geometry. In D. P. Friedman & D. S. Wise (Eds.), Conference record of the 1982 ACM symposium on lisp and functional programming (pp. 179–187). ACM Press.

title: Afterword
text:
The ten-day challenge
The 1446 book closed with a postface, and it made two claims for its little alphabet. The first was that a wise man could learn it before the morning was over, and a slow one within ten days. The second was that it could write down any sound at all: the wind, the cry of a crane, the crowing of a cock, the barking of a dog. This book closes by restating both, because they are its own measures of success.
The first claim was about speed, and you have finished its morning. Here is the rest of the promise. For the next ten days, bring one question a day from your own data, not from the book’s cast of tables, and answer it in one sentence. Start where the cookbook starts: what shape is your data, and what do you want to know? By day three the recipes will read as ordinary sentences, because you will already know every word in them. By day ten you should be writing sentences this book never showed you. That is the one outcome that proves you learned the grammar and not the examples.
Two things count as a surprise. A sentence renders when you expected a refusal, or it refuses and gives you a direction you disagree with. Either is worth reporting, because a grammar this small stays correct only when its readers say where it is wrong.

title: Afterword
text:
Growth without new words
The second claim was about reach: any sound at all. A grammar of graphics answers it in pictures, and the kernel you learned is the whole vocabulary it has. The engine draws every word in it: every mark, every channel, every transform, every space, and the one selection. Not every pairing of words is drawn yet, and Combinations is the page that lists the ones the engine still refuses. No word is waiting.
Growth arrives as new pictures rather than new words. The choropleth is the pattern, and no atom was added for it. It shades each country by a value. What it needed was not a new word but a new shape of table: one row for every point along a country’s border. A zone is a filled region, and five different things can fix where its edges are. A boundary is the fifth, and group already says which rows belong to one country. Map shows the choropleth drawn with the words the kernel already had.
The vocabulary does not grow across languages either. Whatever sentence you write becomes one small specification inside the package, and all four bindings build the same one from the same words. What differs is how each one names a column, and JavaScript spells the operators as words as well, because it cannot overload them. Each binding has a short chapter of its own, a difference list: R, Python, Julia, JavaScript.
# Python
(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life)
  + color(col.continent))
# Julia
data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life) + color(:continent)
// JavaScript
plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life), color(col.continent))

title: Afterword
text:
One goal left
Those four spellings are finished work. One thing this project set out to do is not, and it is written down here so you can check later whether the project did it. Half of it already works: the engine itself runs inside the page, which is how a 3-D plot turns when you drag it in the web edition. The other half is every example in this book, editable in place. Change color(continent) to shape(continent), and watch the plot redraw. The book you are reading is ready for that change today, because it holds no saved pictures: every plot in it comes from a specification the engine reads.

title: Afterword
section: Writing quickly is not writing well
text:
Writing quickly is not writing well
I think Hangeul (한글) is a perfect writing system. I should admit that I may be biased, because it is the alphabet I write with. What nobody disputes is that it is fast to read and fast to write.
Writing quickly is not the same as writing well. There is no quick route to good writing: you read good writing, and you practice. Visualization is no different. This tool is new and it has problems, and what I hope it can be for now is a good tool to practice with.
The same division sits in the 1446 story. King Sejong made the alphabet. He did not write the books that were written with it. I am not a great author of plots either. What I do have is twenty years in this field as a user, watching and listening and reading. I built from that experience, and what came out is a tool that is easy to learn and easy to use.
I hope good work comes out of it.

title: Afterword
text:
The gap
A specification is a sentence said before the picture exists. Everyone who writes one waits in that gap, between declaring what they want to see and finding out whether the engine agrees. The package is gog. The state of working with it is agog. I hope the book kept you there.

Be agog. Use gog.

title: Appendix A — The kernel card
text:
The whole grammar, on one page. The table below is extracted from The kernel each time the book builds. It cannot disagree with the chapter it comes from. Functions that act on a plot instead of joining a sentence are in Functions around the grammar.







Kind
The words




Sources
data query


Marks
point line area bar step interval box ribbon text path rule zone surface edge


Channels
x y z color size shape pattern opacity group label play


Transforms
bin smooth count density proportion sum mean median max min quantile range confidence deviation bounds partition flow layout cluster, and the four collision modifiers, dodge stack jitter repel


Operators
+ layers, * derives, | and / arrange


Scales
linear log time category order


Spaces
flat space polar nest map globe network


Settings
style theme palette


Labels
title x_label y_label z_label


Facets
facet


Selections
brush



The minimum sentence is a source, a mark, and the position channels that mark needs:
data(table) + mark + x(column) + y(column)
The order of + is mostly free: every sentence in this book reads left to right as data, mark, positions, refinements. Inside one layer the mark and its channels may be written in any order. data() comes first, and style() comes after the mark it styles. What the order does change is scope and layering. A channel written before any mark applies to every layer that can accept it. A channel written after a mark belongs to that mark alone. Each later data() applies to the mark written directly after it. Two marks draw in the order you wrote them, so the second sits on top of the first. Which orders matter has all of it in one place.
Deriving is what * does: it puts a transform on a mark, and the mark is always on the left. Two transforms can follow one mark: bar * bin * mean cuts the axis into bands, then averages inside each. They have to divide the work, and each job is filled once, so the order you write them in does not change the picture. Writing them in the order they happen is the convention.
Precedence decides what groups first: * and /, then +, then |. In data(table) + bar * bin + x(a) | facet(g), the transform joins its mark first. The atoms join the plot next, and the facet splits the finished plot last. So a single plot needs no parentheses. A page of plots takes one pair of parentheses around each plot. Julia gives + and | the same precedence, so there the parentheses are what keep each plot whole.
When gog refuses, the message names the rule, and says what to write instead. Illegal means the grammar forbids the sentence you wrote: rewrite it. Unsupported means the grammar allows it and this engine does not draw it: use another atom that renders. Illegal is not the same as unsupported has the rule, and a live refusal of each kind.
When gog assumes instead of refusing, the plot still draws. The message is an assumption: it says what gog decided for you. Read it, and check that the decision was what you meant.

title: Appendix B — Functions around the grammar
text:
B.1 render_svg()
Every word in the kernel belongs to a sentence. point is a mark, x is a channel, bin is a transform, and none of them means anything on its own. They are words, and a word needs a sentence.
The functions in this appendix are not words. They take a plot you have already written and act on it, or they hand you a table to write a sentence about. None of them can be written into a sentence with + or *, and none of them is part of the grammar.
The name alone will not tell you whether a function is a word of the grammar. x_label is a word and joins two words with an underscore, exactly as render_svg does. What separates them is where each one can stand. A word of the grammar stands inside a sentence. The three functions below never do, which is why none of them appears in The kernel card.
The list is short, and each function has a section below, in the order of the table. The first turns a finished plot into text.
A plot is a specification until something draws it. render_svg() takes the plot as its one argument, and it has the same name in all four languages. It draws the plot and gives you the result as ordinary text:

picture <- render_svg(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life))
cat(substr(picture, 1, 51), "\n")

<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" width="800" 

cat(nchar(picture), "characters\n")

14659 characters
The first line of output shows where that text begins. The second line gives its whole length. So the picture you have been looking at is also this: a run of characters that starts <svg and states a width. After that it names every point, every tick and every label.
That text is the whole plot. It is what every notebook, every web page and this book itself shows you. Writing it to a file with a .svg name gives you a picture that any browser opens and a vector drawing program edits.

title: Appendix B — Functions around the grammar
text:
B.1.1 What the file carries
An SVG file is text, so anyone who opens it can read it. If your table holds something private, open the file and read it yourself before you publish. The file carries the drawing and nothing else.
A plot draws the columns you map. Columns you never map are absent from the file, and so are their names:

private <- data.frame(
  patient = c("A. Kim", "B. Lee", "C. Park", "D. Choi"),
  email   = c("ak@ex.com", "bl@ex.com", "cp@ex.com", "dc@ex.com"),
  weight  = c(61.2, 74.8, 55.4, 68.0)
)

picture <- render_svg(data(private) + bar * bin + x(weight))
sapply(c("A. Kim", "email", "ex.com", "61.2"), grepl, x = picture, fixed = TRUE)

A. Kim  email ex.com   61.2 
 FALSE  FALSE  FALSE  FALSE 


Every search returns FALSE. The sentence maps one column, so the drawing used one column. Even the weights are gone, because bin counts rows into intervals and the bars show the counts.
The weights are absent because of the transform, not because a plot never carries values. A mark that summarizes draws no individual row. A mark that does not summarize draws one glyph per row, and each glyph is placed from one value:

picture <- render_svg(data(private) + point + x(weight) + y(patient))
lengths(gregexpr("<circle", picture))

[1] 4


The four rows drew four circles, and the four patient names are printed along the axis. Every plotting tool works this way, and it is what you asked for. A scatter plot draws each value you gave it.
The number itself is not written in the file. Each circle sits where that number puts it, so a reader who measures the drawing can recover the value.
So the rule is not that the file is safe. The real rule is narrower and more useful. What you map is what you publish. A column you never map cannot be recovered from the file, and a private column the sentence never names stays private.


B.1.2 Plots that carry the table
One case works differently, and you should know it before you publish.
Some plots are drawn twice. You make the first drawing. The reader’s browser makes the second, because the reader can move a selection or turn the view. Four kinds of plot do this: one that binds brush(), one in the cube, one on the globe, and a network given an angle. The second drawing needs the numbers, so the page carries the table beside the picture.
It carries the whole table, including columns the sentence never maps. show rows is a button under the plot, explained in Selection. The table it opens lists only the mapped columns. The page itself carries every column.
The remedy is to bind a table that holds only the columns you plot. Here is private again with the email column left out:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


shown <- data.frame(
  patient = c("A. Kim", "B. Lee", "C. Park", "D. Choi"),
  weight  = c(61.2, 74.8, 55.4, 68.0)
)

“Given the shown table: points, x is weight, y is patient, and let the reader select weight.”
That sentence names a brush, so this page carries a table. The table it carries is shown, which has two columns. If you bound private instead, email would be on this page too. Each language has its own way to drop a column from a table before you bind it, and that work belongs to the language rather than to the grammar.
An SVG file never carries the table, even when its sentence names a brush. render_svg() gives you the picture and stops.


B.1.3 What “byte for byte” means
This book says in several places that the four languages draw the same picture byte for byte. That claim is about render_svg(), and the idea is simple.
A plot looks like a picture on your screen. Underneath, it is the text that render_svg() returns. Two plots are the same when that text is the same, byte for byte. Not similar. Not close enough to look the same. The same.
That is how the four languages are kept the same. Nearly every sentence in this book is written in R, in Python, in Julia and in JavaScript. Each one that draws is turned into its text, and the four texts are compared one byte at a time. One wrong byte counts as a disagreement and has to be explained.
A test that allowed small differences would accept pictures that are not the same. Nobody looks at four pictures and decides whether they match. A person cannot see a bar that is half a pixel too wide, or a color that is slightly wrong. Comparing the text finds both differences, and it works the same way every time.

title: Appendix B — Functions around the grammar
text:
B.3 gog_table()
render_svg() and save_gif() act on a finished plot. This one comes before the plot. Every shared table this book plots is available to you by name, so you can run any example here without downloading a file first:
gapminder_2007 <- gog_table("gapminder_2007")
data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life)
That block does not run on this page, and the reason is worth one line. The call reads the table over the network. If the book did that on every build, it could not render without a connection.
gog_table() exists for reading this book rather than for your own work. When the data is yours, bind it with data() and skip gog_table() entirely.
The book’s data is the chapter for this function. It lists every table in the book and shows the call in each of the four languages.

title: Appendix C — Combinations
text:
C.1 Marks and channels
Every mark down the side, every channel across the top: the whole of what the grammar lets you combine, on one page. This page holds four crossings. The first is what a mark lets you map, which is the channels. The second is what a mark lets you derive, which is the transforms. The third is which two transforms can stand together on one mark. The fourth is where a mark can be drawn, which is the coordinate spaces. Each one shows what a mark takes, what it does not, and the surprising pairings that are legal anyway.
These grids are the orthogonality law made visible. Law 1 says every compatible atom combines with every other; a table is that promise enumerated, one cell at a time. It is the direct analog of the letter chart a Hangeul (한글) learner reads, with the consonants down one side and the vowels across the top. A syllable block is what those letters assemble into. This book has used that pairing from the start: a mark is a consonant and a position is a vowel, and neither draws alone. Every syllable the grammar can form appears somewhere in the crossing.
Legal is not the same as useful. Law 8, Pronounceable ≠ Usable, guarantees only that the engine draws what a cell allows. Whether it should be drawn is your judgment. A cell the engine refuses teaches as much as one it draws. It records a real limit of the geometry, not an oversight.
Every grid here is generated live from the engine’s own rule table, each time the book builds. That is the same table the engine consults to accept or refuse your plot. A grid that is described can stop matching the code; a grid that is generated cannot. Add a mark, a channel, a transform or a space and these pages widen by themselves.
Take the channels first. Each cell says whether you may map a column to that channel on that mark.
Reading the five glyphs:
Five things the grid shows that prose has to say one at a time:

● must: a required position. The mark does not render without it. A point needs an x and a y; a text needs its label.
✅ maps: bind a column here and the engine draws it today. This is the ordinary case, a channel doing its job.
○ set: the mark has this feature, but not row by row. A line is one stroke, so its size and opacity are a single value for the whole layer, fixed with style() rather than mapped. Those constants have their own Mark × Setting grid. Seven of them never appear on this grid at all: border_color, border_size, caps, center, nudge, arrow and reach are settings and nothing else. Two questions, not one puts both halves in one table.
◌ not drawn: legal grammar the engine refuses today. It gives you a direction instead of a wrong picture. One glyph, three verdicts, and the refusal message tells you which you have. Owed: a mapped size or opacity on text, z on text, and pattern on edge. Blocked on infrastructure: z on rule and on zone. Their 3-D forms are a plane and a slab with no footprint to sort by, so they need an engine that can tell what hides what. Decided: z on line, step, area and ribbon. These marks read a domain from left to right, and a cube has no left to right, so the refusal points to path instead. The Mark × Space grid below is the same three readings on its own blanks.
— none: the mark has no such feature. A bar has no glyph to shape, and a point has no line to group into. Binding it means nothing, and the engine says so.



group splits a line, not a bar. Read down the group column: — on the five marks that draw one shape per row (point, bar, text, rule, edge), ✅ on every mark that builds one shape out of many rows. A bar is split into groups by color, then piled or set side by side with stack / dodge. A bare group has no line to divide.
label belongs to text alone. Its column is ● on text and — everywhere else. A labeled scatter is the superposition point + text, never a label hung on the point.
Categories on x and on y. A category on x reaches every mark that has positions except surface, and on y it reaches fewer of them. Read the x and y columns against each other. Which types each accepts is in Channels, and the split divides the marks with positions in two. The glyph marks (point, text) and the marks whose slot width does the measuring (bar, interval, box) take either type on both positions. That one rule is where a strip plot, a horizontal bar and a categorical box all come from. Three more marks do the same. A path sorts nothing, so it has no domain. A rule measures nothing on either axis. A zone measures nothing by length, and that is what makes a heatmap cell a zone rather than a second kind of bar. The path and region marks (line, step, area, ribbon) take either type on x alone. Their x is the domain the path is read along, and their y is the quantity it traces. Those are two different kinds of axis. A glyph’s two axes are the same kind, which is why a point and a text take either type on both. surface stands outside the split, because both of its positions measure. A sheet is a height, and the two positions say where that height is read.
Three rows have no ● at all. rule and zone show ✅ on both positions and ● on neither, because each needs one of the two and no per-channel cell can say “either, but not both”. edge is the third, and it takes no position at all. Those obligations are stated once in the engine instead. Two ✅s on the positions and no ● means the mark needs one of them, and the panel supplies the other (Rule, Zone).
zone and surface take either type on color. They are the two fills that do: every other region’s fill takes a category, and these two take a number as well, reading the ramp.

C.2 Marks and transforms
The second crossing: not what a mark maps, but what it derives. A transform enters through * (bar * bin, interval * range, point * jitter), and which transform a mark takes is decided by the mark’s geometry against the transform’s kind. There are three kinds, and each has its own grid below.
Three glyphs read every cell:

✅ combines: the transform applies to this mark and renders.
● required: the mark will not draw until a transform of this kind is present, so that kind is part of its minimum syllable. An interval and a ribbon span a low value and a high one, so neither draws until one transform of that kind supplies the pair. The ● cells in a row are a choice, not a list: pick one. A zone shows ● wherever a transform is one of the ways it gets its sides.
— none: the mark has no use for this kind of transform, and the engine refuses it with a direction toward the transform its geometry does want.


C.2.1 Statistics: a value per group
The first of the three kinds is also the largest. Most summarizing transforms reduce the data to one value at each x: a bin’s count, a group’s mean, a smoothed height. Any mark that draws a value at each x can draw that summary, so those marks are ✅ under every summary. That is why a distribution has three spellings rather than one histogram with a shape option: bar * bin fills it, line * bin is the frequency polygon, step * bin the staircase.

A box carries its own summary: the five numbers come from the mark itself rather than from a transform you compose, so no statistic column applies to it. Each has a chapter of its own.

An interval and a ribbon have no baseline to start from, so neither renders until a pair transform gives it a low and a high. interval * range is the whole minimum syllable, and a bare interval is refused. C.2.3 Collision modifiers: an offset, not a statistic
When marks collide at one position, four offsets separate them, and which one a mark takes is decided by its geometry and by the axis the collision is on. dodge subdivides a width, so it serves the marks that have one (bar, box, interval). stack accumulates along the measure axis, so it serves the marks that can spend a span. bar and area fill that span with length. A point has no length of its own, so it spends the span on counting dots instead, which is the dot plot. jitter spreads a mark with no width along a categorical axis, which is point alone. repel divides on a different question: not what geometry a mark has, but what it is made of. A label is as wide as the word it draws, so two labels overlap where their points do not, and text is the only mark made of words.

C.3 Transforms and transforms
The third crossing is the only one where a mark does not appear. Two transforms can follow one mark: bar * bin * mean cuts the axis into bands, then averages inside each. Which pairs can do that is decided by the transforms alone, and by one rule.
A transform has a job. There are four of them, and every transform in gog fills at least one, except repel:








job
the question it answers
the transforms that answer it




extent
where are the cells?
bin, density, smooth, partition, and bounds on a zone


measure
what is in them?
count, sum, mean, median, max, min, quantile, range, confidence, deviation, bounds


scale
what scale is the answer read on?
proportion, and stack(share = TRUE)


position
where do the marks sit?
dodge, stack, jitter



repel fills no job at all. It moves a label after every job has run, so it contradicts nothing. Its row in the grid below is the only one that is ✅ from end to end, and that includes the other three offsets. flow, layout and cluster fill all four jobs at once. Each computes the whole picture, so repel is the only transform that can follow one.
Two transforms compose when they do different jobs, and contradict when they do the same one. Each of those cells holds one extent, one measure, one scale and one position. So a second transform doing a job the first already did leaves the engine no reading that keeps both, and it refuses rather than drawing one and discarding the other.
One transform is the exception, and it is the exception that makes chaining useful. bin does two jobs: it cuts the axis, and it counts what lands in each band. The count is a by-product of the cut, so bin does not have to keep it. It hands the measure job to any transform you gave a column. The other extent transforms do two jobs as well, and none of them can do the same. A density or a smooth cell is a point on an estimated curve, which sits between the rows rather than holding any of them, so there is nothing inside it to reduce. That is why bar * bin * mean composes: bin supplies the cells and mean supplies their value. And it is why bar * bin * count does not, since count was never handed a column to reduce.

The grid is symmetric, and the reason is in the rule rather than in the drawing. Whether two transforms contradict is a fact about their jobs, and it has nothing to do with which one you typed first. So the order is yours to choose. Write the transforms in the order they run, and the sentence reads in that order too.
Read the block of — in the middle of the grid. Eleven transforms measure, so no two of them combine. That block is the whole reason bar * count * mean is refused, and bar * mean * sum, and interval * range * confidence. Now compare bin’s row with smooth’s and density’s. Those two chain with no measure transform at all, and bin chains with ten. That is the exception above, written out in the grid.
Two collisions the grid cannot show, because both depend on something outside the pair. stack(share = TRUE) divides each pile by its own total, which is a scale. proportion divides again, and the second division has no whole left to be a share of. And bounds says where a zone’s sides are. On that one mark it does the extent job, so it contradicts bin. On every other mark it names the low and the high on the measure axis. The engine reads both cases correctly, and the grid above shows the reading that applies everywhere else.
Chaining stops at four, and nobody chose the number. There are four jobs and one transform fills each of them, so a fifth transform has to repeat a job on the same mark. Repeating one is the contradiction this whole section is about.

C.3.1 The shapes a long chain can take
The rule above allows chains of three and four, so it is fair to ask how many there are. The answer is a short list. Once each job is filled at most once, and the marks are asked which transforms they take, every chain of three or four takes one of the shapes below. Two slots stand for a family rather than a transform: <aggregation> is any of sum, mean, median, max, min, quantile, and <collision modifier> is dodge, stack or jitter, whichever the mark takes.

Read the four-transform row first, because it is the longest chain there is. It fills each job exactly once, and two of its four slots are decided before you choose anything. bin is the only extent transform that gives its measurement to another, and proportion is the only one that rescales. That leaves two choices: the aggregation, which is free among six, and the offset, which the mark narrows to one or two. Four is reachable, and this is why it is rare.
The shapes say what the transforms allow. A mark can still refuse one of them for a reason about its own geometry, and the grids earlier in this chapter are where that is decided. point * proportion * stack is the clearest case. A dot plot piles one whole dot per observation, and a share is less than one dot. So the chain is refused on point and drawn on bar.

title: Appendix C — Combinations

C.4 Marks and spaces
The fourth crossing is not a channel of the mark at all. It is the coordinate space the whole plot sits in, and it asks a different question of every mark. Once the plane is bent, or turned into a cube, can this geometry still be drawn? A polar() bar is a wedge, a polar() line is a closed curve, and a z scatter is a projected cloud, all from the same sentences that draw them flat.
Two glyphs here, not five. Either the engine draws this mark in this space today, or it does not and says so:

✅ drawn: the mark renders in this space.
— not drawn: legal to write and refused with direction, never half-drawn. As on the channel grid, one glyph stands for owed, blocked and decided alike. The paragraphs under the table say which one each blank is.

flat is full but for surface and edge, and surface is the one to read first: it does not draw in the plane at all. Every other mark draws there, and some also draw in the cube. A surface is a sheet through three positions, and there is no such thing without the third, so its minimum syllable includes the cube. It is the only mark that draws in the cube and not in the plane (Surface). An edge is the other kind of blank, and it is blank in every column but the last. It takes no position at all, so the only space that can draw it is the one that places its nodes. Read the columns that follow with edge set aside.
space holds six marks, and the six follow from one reading rather than from a list. A point is a place, a path is an order, a surface is a sheet. bar, interval and box are the three marks that stand in a slot and measure along the other axis: a length, a span and a summary, which the grammar treats as one family. Each means in a cube exactly what it meant on the page.
The blanks in that column are not one kind of thing, and the refusal message says which each is. line, step, area and ribbon read a domain left to right, and a cube has no left to right. So they are decided, a ruling rather than work still owed, and the refusal points to path instead. rule and zone are blocked, the same reading their z cells carry. A plane and a slab have no footprint to sort by, so placing them among the data needs an engine that can tell what hides what (Space). text is owed: a label in the cube is not built yet, and the message says so rather than drawing one flat (Space).
polar matches flat: the same twelve marks draw, and the same two do not. Every mark that draws on the page also draws in the circle. Bending the plane only curves a mark’s edges, and every flat mark has edges that can curve. A band’s boundaries are the same chords a line draws. The two blanks are surface and edge, and neither is a polar refusal: a sheet needs the cube, and an edge needs the space that places its nodes (Polar).
nest is a column of the opposite shape: two cells filled and the rest blank. Those blanks are not work waiting to be done. This space asks a different question from the other five. Everywhere else a mark bends because its geometry survives a transformation of the plane. A nesting is not a transformation of the plane at all, so it can draw any mark that accepts a rectangle. A bar accepts one, because a bar is a measure. A measure has been a length on the page and an angle in the circle, and here it becomes the size of a rectangle. text can take one too, and it is the only mark here that names a region rather than filling one. The rectangle is already computed, so the label goes to its center. That is what a published treemap has, and what a legend cannot do once the split runs past a hundred regions (Nest).
The blanks share one reason, and it is not that the space is unfinished. They are the marks placed by a position. point needs somewhere to sit. line, step, path, area and ribbon need an order along an axis, and two touching regions here are not near each other in the data. rule and zone span an axis that is not there, and box, interval and surface measure along one. edge is placed by a layout that this space does not compute. text is missing from that list because no position places it here. The region places it, and the region is what places the bar too.
map, the sixth column, fills five cells, and the shape of its column comes from one fact: longitude and latitude spend both positions on the place. The marks that draw are the ones that place something. A point is a place, a path is a route, and a text is a name at a place. A rule at one position spans the other, which makes it a meridian or a parallel. A zone takes its sides from a boundary, which is the choropleth (Map). The blanks share one reason: each of them needs an axis of its own, either to measure along or to read a domain along, and a map has neither to give. The quantity moves to size or color instead, which is what cartography does with a measure once both positions are gone.
globe, the column before it, fills six cells. Five of them are map’s five, and the sixth is one a flat map cannot have. The sphere and its flattening answer one question: where does a place go. So the marks that place something stand on both, and only the reader’s view changes. The far half of the earth is hidden behind the sphere, a route bends along a great circle, and a rule becomes the whole meridian or parallel it holds. The sixth cell is bar, because the sphere alone has a direction to spare: the radius, which runs straight out from the surface at every place. A bar drawn along it is a spike, with z naming its measure (Globe). The blanks are map’s, minus that bar, and they are blank for the same reason. A sphere has no axis of its own to give them either.
network holds three cells, and one of its marks draws in no other space. edge draws nowhere else, because an edge is placed by neither position: the space computes where every node sits and the edge follows the two it joins (Network). point and text join it there, as the nodes and their names.
Three of the four crossings have a mark on every row, so one mark can be read across all three at once. A path takes nearly every channel on Mark × Channel and almost nothing on Mark × Transform, because a path is its rows in order and every statistic replaces them. rule reads the same way on the transform grid, and for the reason the statistics grid already gave: it hands a whole axis to the panel, so it has no measure to compute. And surface has a row of the transforms that cover a plane. density estimates a value at every node and bin cuts adjacent cells, while sum, mean, median, max and min name the column each cell holds. path derives two things. With density it draws the contour of a field, the same field a surface lifts into a sheet. With cluster it draws the tree.
With these grids the orthogonality law is stated in full: what each mark maps, what it sets (the Mark × Setting grid), what it derives, and where it can be drawn.

title: Appendix D — Chart names, translated
text:
D.1 Names with a one-line answer
gog has no chart-type atoms: a histogram is a sentence, not a word. But people look for plots by name, so this appendix is the index of names. It is the one place organized by chart name. The cookbook covers the same plots organized by question, which is usually the better place to start.
Column names here are placeholders. Replace them with your own.
Each of these names is one gog sentence. The left column is the name you know, and the right column is the sentence that draws it. Where a name needs a second word, it follows the sentence in the same cell.

title: Appendix D — Chart names, translated
text:
The name you know
The sentence




Scatter plot
point + x(a) + y(b)


Bubble chart
point + x(a) + y(b) + size(c)


Strip plot
point + x(category) + y(measure), or swap the axes to draw it sideways


Bar chart
bar + x(category) + y(measure)


Horizontal bar chart
bar + x(measure) + y(category)


Hatched (print-safe) bars
bar + x(category) + y(measure) + style(pattern = "hatch"), also "crosshatch"/"stripes"/"grid"/"dots"


Count (frequency) chart
bar * count + x(category)


Proportion chart
bar * proportion + x(category)


Histogram
bar * bin + x(measure); bin(30) sets the number of bins and bin(width = 5) sets their width


Frequency polygon
line * bin + x(measure)


Outline (step) histogram
step * bin + x(measure)


Overlaid histograms
bar * bin + x(measure) + color(group)


Density plot
line * density + x(measure)


Line chart / time series
line + x(time) + y(measure)


Multi-series lines by dash (no color)
line + x(time) + y(measure) + pattern(series), add color(series) for redundant encoding


Step chart
step + x(a) + y(b)


Empirical CDF
step over cumulative shares, worked example in Step


Area chart
area + x(a) + y(b)


Spread / range band
ribbon * range + x(a) + y(b), split by group with color(group)


Confidence band (computed)
ribbon * confidence(0.95) + x(a) + y(b), often under a line * mean trend


Confidence band (pre-computed)
ribbon * bounds(lower, upper) + x(a), bounds you already have (a model’s standard error, a standard error of measurement)


Unfilled (dashed) error band
line * bounds(lower, upper) + x(a) + style(pattern = "dashed"), the upper and lower edges drawn as two lines, with nothing filled between them


Min–max envelope, as two lines
line * range + x(a) + y(b), the unfilled counterpart to ribbon * range


Dashed / dotted line
any line/step + style(pattern = "dashed") (or "dotted")


Trend line / smoother / LOESS
line * smooth + x(a) + y(b)


Summary bars (mean per group)
bar * mean + x(category) + y(measure), also sum, median, max, min


Grouped bars (side by side)
bar * mean * dodge + x(category) + y(measure) + color(group), where * dodge gives each group its own bar side by side inside the category’s slot


Colorblind-safe grouped bars
add + pattern(group) to the grouped bars: one column drives both the color and the hatch, so the two share one merged legend


Ranked bars
add + order(measure, desc = TRUE)


Small multiples / trellis / conditioning plot / facets
plot \| facet(category), plot / facet(category), or both for a grid


Small multiples of 3-D plots
any cube sentence \| facet(category): each panel holds its own cube, all drawn from the same angle


3-D scatter
point + x(a) + y(b) + z(c), view angle via space(turn = , tilt = )


3-D trajectory / space curve
path + x(a) + y(b) + z(c), the rows joined in table order, in the cube


Surface plot / wireframe
surface + x(a) + y(b) + z(c) over a table with one row per (x, y) crossing, every a value paired with every b value; style(border_color = "white") draws the mesh lines, color(c) shades it by height


Terrain / elevation / bathymetry
the same sentence: a height over a plane is a surface, whatever the height means


Response surface
surface + x(factor1) + y(factor2) + z(response) over the design grid; from a fitted model, predict onto a grid first and name that table in the sentence


3-D density surface
surface * density + x(a) + y(b) + space(), the estimate raised as height. That is the third geometry of one field, which zone * density paints and path * density traces


Profile plot (categories joined)
line * mean + x(category) + y(measure), one summary per category with the path across them; step stays flat between categories instead of sloping


Filled profile
area * mean + x(category) + y(measure), the same boundary filled to the baseline


Connected scatterplot
path + x(a) + y(b), the rows joined in the table’s order rather than sorted by x; style(arrow = "end") says which end is last


Trajectory / route / hysteresis loop
the same sentence: any reading whose order is the data’s is path, not line


Annotation arrow / callout
data(two_rows) + path + style(arrow = "end"), layered over the plot; the note itself is data(one_row) + text + label(note)


Rose / coxcomb / wind rose
bar * count + x(direction) + polar(), the bar chart read in a circle


Radar / spider plot
line * mean + x(category) + y(measure) + polar(), the profile bent into a circle; area fills it


Pie chart
bar * count * stack + color(category) + polar(), a stacked bar in polar coordinates; the category is a split, not a position


Sunburst
zone * partition(a, b, c) + x(measure) + polar(), worked example in Polar. One ring per level of a tree, each arc as wide as its share. The hierarchy is columns, outermost first. A blank level ends that branch early, so the branch stops short of the outer ring. That is what makes the rim ragged. y(depth, limits = c(0, n)) puts the hole in the middle, and text * partition(…) + label(name) names the nodes, reading the same centers the zone computed


Icicle / partition chart
the sunburst’s sentence with polar() taken off, which is the whole difference: depth up the y axis, share across the x. The two names are one coordinate space apart, exactly as a rose and a bar chart are, or a pie and a stacked bar


Treemap
bar * sum + y(value) + color(category) + nest(), the same shares carried by area rather than by angle (Nest)


Nested treemap
the same, plus x(group): one region per group, its rows packed inside


Labeled treemap
the same, plus a text layer: + text + label(name) writes each region’s name at its center, which is what a packing needs once the split has too many levels for a legend. A name wider than its own region is left out, and the plot reports how many names it dropped (Nest)


Pie of a measure
bar * sum * stack + y(amount) + color(category) + polar(), also proportion for shares on the axis


Share-of-total column
the same sentence without polar(), one segmented bar


Polar histogram
bar * bin + x(bearing) + polar(), bins as wedges of a measured angle


Circular (cyclical) line
line + x(hour) + y(measure) + polar(), both ends of the cycle in the data


Polar scatter
point + x(bearing) + y(measure) + polar()


Contour plot / density contours
path * density + x(a) + y(b), the contours of a density estimated over the plane; density(levels = ) says how many, group(category) estimates one field per group. zone * density(levels = ) fills one band per level, on the levels the contours trace. The filled reading draws one field wrongly: a crater, which is a ring-shaped cluster with a hollow middle. A band around a hollow is a shape with a hole, and gog has no mark for one


2-D density heatmap
zone * density + x(a) + y(b), the same field painted as cells instead of traced as lines


Filled contour / filled density
zone * density(levels = 8) + x(a) + y(b), eight bands, one per level; the same levels a path traces


Binned heatmap
zone * bin + x(a) + y(b), cells colored by how many rows fell in each


Hexbin
zone * bin(tiling = "hex") + x(a) + y(b), a staggered mesh, whose cells form no straight rows or columns for a reader to mistake for structure in the data


Heat strip / binned distribution per group
zone * bin + x(number) + y(category), the mixed mesh: the continuous axis cut into cells, one row of cells per category. Every row is cut on the same edges, so the cells line up down the plot


Choropleth
zone with group(country) and map(): group says which rows belong to one region, and the region’s own boundary becomes the zone’s sides (Map)


Candlestick / OHLC chart
two layers over one table, worked example in Zone: interval * bounds(low, high) + color(dir) is the whisker and zone * bounds(body_lo, body_hi, start = left, end = right) + color(dir) + style(opacity = 1) the body, over x(session). Four numbers a session, and no new channel for them. bounds reads a low value and a high value, and a rectangle’s bottom and top are the same two numbers. The opacity and the named sides both replace a zone default meant for highlighting: here the rectangle is the data


Waterfall / bridge chart
zone * bounds(base, top, start = left, end = right) + x(step) + color(dir) + style(opacity = 1), worked example in Zone. stack accumulates within a position and a waterfall accumulates across positions, so the running total is arithmetic that belongs with the data, in the host language. The subtotal bars start at 0. left and right sit just inside each slot’s edges, which is what leaves a gap between the bars


Funnel chart
zone * bounds(lo, hi) + y(stage) + style(opacity = 1), worked example in Zone, with text + label(n) + x(mid) for the numbers inside. The columns lo and hi hold -n/2 and n/2, computed in the host, which is the same arithmetic the waterfall uses for its running total. A funnel is a bar chart whose blocks are centered on zero. Centering is arithmetic on two columns, so a funnel is not a chart type. The measure goes on x because y(stage) is a category. Nothing in the sentence has to ask for that, because the kinds of the columns settle it. gog draws no sloped connectors between the stages, on purpose. A connector spans the gap between two categories. That gap carries no values, so no scale can give its width a meaning

title: Appendix D — Chart names, translated
text:
D.2 Names that need more
These names need a paragraph rather than a line. All but one of them draw, and the entry gives the sentence. Where one does not, the entry says so first, and then says what the closest sentence leaves out.



The name
The sentence, and what to know




Box plot
box + x(group) + y(value), the five-number summary per group


Violin plot
ribbon * density + x(group) + y(value), the shape the box plot’s five numbers summarize. density(compare = ) says whether the widths carry each group’s row count (the default) or draw every violin to the same area


Half violin
area * density + x(group) + y(value): the same estimate, closed on the slot’s center line instead of on its own mirror image. That is what separates area from ribbon everywhere in the book


Ridgeline plot / joyplot
area * density(reach = 2.5) + x(value) + y(group), the half violin with its axes exchanged, one density per category, each on its own line, sharing one measure axis. reach is in slots, so past 0.5 the ridges leave their own slots, which is what makes a joyplot. To outline it, add a layer: line * density + style(color = "black") reads the same estimate and traces the top of the fill


Jittered strip plot
point * jitter + x(group) + y(value), the jitter collision modifier spreads coincident points along the category axis


Labeled scatter, names not overlapping
point + text * repel + x(a) + y(b) + label(name), where the repel collision modifier moves each word off the other words and off the dots. When a label has moved far, repel draws a thin line back to its point


Stacked bars / areas
bar * sum * stack / area * sum * stack with a color split, the stack collision modifier (grouped bars are its sibling dodge)


100% stacked bar / filled area
bar * count * stack(share = TRUE) + x(a) + color(b), every pile is divided by its own slot’s total. Each pile then reaches 1, so the plot shows composition and no longer shows size. Any measurement fills the same way, sum included


Streamgraph
area * stack(baseline = "wiggle") + x(t) + y(v) + color(g), worked example in Transforms. The foot of each pile is placed to keep the bands as flat as possible, so a band’s shape is its own rather than the sum of everything below it. share and baseline are the pile’s two independent choices, and you can use them together


ThemeRiver
area * stack(baseline = "center"), the same sentence with the symmetric layout instead (Havre et al., 2000). Often confused with the streamgraph and not the same plot: this one centers every pile, and the streamgraph keeps its bands as flat as possible. The streamgraph’s designers argue that readers compare values more accurately on it (Byron & Wattenberg, 2008)


Alluvial diagram
ribbon * flow(a, b, c) + y(count), with zone * flow(...) for the stage slots and text * flow(...) + label(name) for their names, worked example in Flow. One row of the table is one path through the stages. Between each pair of neighboring stages, one band carries that path’s size


Sankey diagram
Not drawn in the general form. The alluvial draws the same merged bands. Reduce the table to one pair of stages at a time, and each band is the flow between that pair. The general many-source form, given as a list of nodes and a list of links, is a different input shape and is not read (Flow says where the limits are)


Network diagram / node-link graph
edge * layout(from, to) + network(), with point * layout(...) for the nodes, size(degree) sizing each node by its relations, and text * layout(...) + label(name) for their names, worked example in Network. The engine computes every position, so the picture is the same in all four languages. State an angle, network(turn = 35, tilt = 20), and the same layout becomes a cube the reader can drag in the web edition


Relative-frequency histogram
bar * bin * proportion + x(number), the histogram’s own counts read as fractions of n, on the mesh bar * bin cuts


Heatmap
A heatmap is drawn on two continuous axes, on two categorical axes, or on one of each. The transform you need depends on which kinds you have. A continuous axis needs cutting, so zone * bin counts the rows per cell: both axes for the classic heatmap, one for the mixed mesh. A categorical axis arrives cut, so on two of them zone * count tallies into the slots, and zone + color(value) draws a table you already have. zone * density is the third route, and it estimates a value at each cell of a plane rather than counting rows


Summary heatmap / matrix of means
zone * mean + x(a) + y(b) + color(column) reduces the named column within every cell two categories cross, and sum/median/max/min read the same mesh. The column is named on color because that is the channel a zone measures with. A summary reduces in place, so the channel that names the column also receives the result, exactly as y does on bar * mean + x + y


Tile plot / calendar heatmap
zone + x(a) + y(b) + color(value), one cell per pair of categories, filling the slot each one owns


Confusion matrix
zone * count + x(actual) + y(predicted) tallies the raw rows; zone * proportion reads them as shares of the whole. Normalizing per true class, a share within each row of the grid, is not one of these: stack(share = ) divides a pile by its slot’s total, and a grid has no pile to divide


Correlation matrix / corrplot
Drawn as a tile plot, once the correlations are a table. Compute them where your data lives, then reshape the result so that each row holds one pair of variables and their correlation. zone + x(var1) + y(var2) + color(r) draws that table. gog computes no correlations, and that is the host language’s job. A channel names a column; it does not compute one


Donut chart
zone * partition(category) + x(measure) + y(depth, limits = c(0, 2)) + polar(), worked example in Polar. A donut is a sunburst of a tree one level deep. The hole is not a shape that gog draws. It is a stretch of the radial axis with nothing standing on it, which is what the stated limits leave empty. The plain pie (bar * count * stack) is the one reading that cannot ask for a hole. It measures with the angle, so its radius is a constant and has no domain to widen. That is a fact about the reading rather than a gap, so there is no polar(hole = ) and no plan for one


Animated (time-lapse) chart
any sentence + play(year): faceting read in time


Marginal / joint plot (scatter with histograms in its margins)
top / (main | right): three ordinary plots and the two composition operators. There is no chart type and no ggMarginal(). The marginals align and share their scale because both name the same column on the same axis. That shared scale is the one thing composition adds (Composition). Any mark can be the marginal: a histogram, a box, a violin, a dot plot


Dendrogram / cluster tree
path * cluster(value, over = profile) + x(item) joins the closest leaves one pair at a time, and each join’s distance goes on an axis of its own. item is the column that names the leaves, and binding it to y instead lays the tree on its side (Cluster). Dendrogram is Greek for tree drawing, which is what cluster tree says in English


Clustered heatmap
zone * cluster(over = profile) reorders a tile plot’s slots into the tree’s leaf order. The full figure is the marginal plot, with one tree over the tiles and one beside them, and each shared axis takes its tree’s order (Cluster)


3-D surface
The same sentence as Surface plot / wireframe in the first table, surface + x(a) + y(b) + z(c) over a grid table, or surface * density + x(a) + y(b) + space() to raise an estimated field. A scatter cannot be one. It is refused toward point rather than drawn as an empty sheet, because a surface’s faces span the gaps between its samples. A surface needs its samples on a grid


Terraced / stepped surface (one value per cell)
surface * bin * mean + x(a) + y(b) + z(v) cuts the floor into cells and lays a flat plateau on each, with a vertical face at every step. This is the sentence for a design that measures one number per condition. An interpolated sheet would claim a gradient nobody observed (Surface)



If the name you are looking for is in neither table, it is usually one of the listed plots drawn with different settings. Ask what question the chart answers, and start from the cookbook. If the name is one of ggplot2’s function names, Coverage lists the same plots, indexed that way. It sorts each name into four: refused, the host language’s job, missing with the direction settled, and not decided either way.




Byron, L., & Wattenberg, M. (2008). Stacked graphs – geometry & aesthetics. IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics, 14(6), 1245–1252. https://doi.org/10.1109/TVCG.2008.166


Havre, S., Hetzler, B., & Nowell, L. (2000). ThemeRiver: Visualizing theme changes over time. Proceedings of the IEEE Symposium on Information Visualization 2000, 115–123. https://doi.org/10.1109/INFVIS.2000.885098

title: Appendix E — The ggplot2 phrasebook
text:
E.1 Side by side
ggplot2 proved that a grammar of graphics could be a working tool and not only a theory. Most readers of this book already know it. gog follows the same grammar and decides the details differently. This appendix covers both: which word to write, and what behaves differently.
The translations assume gog can draw the plot you want. To find out whether it can, read Coverage. That appendix reads ggplot2’s whole reference index against the kernel, in both directions: what gog draws that ggplot2 does not, and what ggplot2 draws that gog does not.
This first table compares the two systems as a whole, rather than word for word.

title: Appendix E — The ggplot2 phrasebook
text:
E.3 Six differences to expect
The words translate, but six things behave differently once they are in place.

+ is still +, and on purpose. ggplot2’s author has said the pipe would have been the better interface (Wickham, 2018). gog kept + for two reasons. Python has no pipe operator of its own, so a pipe could not spell one syntax in all four languages. A pipe also makes every atom a function, and bar * bin has no meaning once both sides are functions. Operators covers this in full, including which atoms commute in gog and did not commute in ggplot2.
Nothing is computed unless you name it. bar draws your numbers unchanged. geom_bar() counts rows on its own, and gog counts only when you write bar * count.
There is one spelling. No geom/stat pairs, and no choice of which function to use. If you can spell one plot two ways here, one of them is a bug. Report it as an issue on the book’s repository.
The scale belongs to the binding. You name a channel once, and its scale is a property of that binding. There is no second atom that names the channel again.
Setting is not mapping. A constant maps no column, so it earns no legend. Write it in style(). In ggplot2 aes(color = "red") is legal and draws a legend with one entry called “red”. Here color("red") asks for a column called red, so gog refuses it and names style(color = "red") as the fix.
Refusals name the fix. A sentence gog cannot draw is refused, and the message names the sentence it would accept. Where you are used to a warning and a plot, gog stops and draws nothing. This book shows refusals on purpose: it runs the refused sentence and prints the message you would see.





Wickham, H. (2018). Answer on why ggplot2 uses + rather than the pipe. Posit (RStudio) Community forum, 29 January 2018.

title: Appendix F — Coverage, both directions
text:
F.1 What gog draws that ggplot2 does not
The phrasebook answers “how do I spell this in gog”. This appendix answers the question underneath it: can it be spelled. Every entry in ggplot2’s reference index was read against the kernel. The result is two lists of very different lengths, and a table of differences between them.
Each table below has a ggplot2 column, and it is dated on purpose, because nothing here can check it: reference index of ggplot2 4.0.3, read 2026-07-26 (Wickham et al., 2026). Every gog claim below is either a live plot on this page or a refusal the build re-runs, and ggplot2 is deliberately not a dependency of this book, so its column is the one that can go out of date.
The short list is the one people expect to be long, so it goes first. The long list is the interesting one, because every item on it is one of four things, and three of the four were decided on purpose.
Two of these are pictures ggplot2 cannot draw. The third is about the vocabulary rather than about a picture.
